essays.title: Human-caused threats create a clear duty

paragraphs.text: Every year, conservation agencies must decide which of thousands of threatened species will receive their limited money and attention.
The policy under discussion offers a simple rule for these choices: society should make efforts to save endangered species only when human activities are the cause of their potential extinction.
I largely support this policy, as long as "human activities" is read broadly enough to include indirect harms such as climate change and introduced diseases.

This position rests on three considerations: the policy assigns responsibility fairly, it directs scarce resources where they are most likely to work, and its main weakness, though real, can be managed.
First, implementing the policy would place the burden of rescue on those who created the danger, a principle we already accept in other areas of life.
When a factory pollutes a river, we do not ask the fishermen downstream to clean it; we require the factory to stop and to repair the damage.

Likewise, when logging, hunting or the illegal wildlife trade pushes an animal toward extinction, it is reasonable to ask society, which [[reaps|reap]] the benefits of those activities, to pay for the recovery.

Similarly, a country that drains a wetland for rice farming has a stronger duty to protect the birds that lived there than a country whose birds are disappearing because of a natural shift in climate.
This shows that the policy's central condition is not arbitrary: it links the duty to act with the act that caused the harm, which makes the duty easier to justify and to enforce.
Second, the policy would likely make conservation more effective, because threats caused by humans are usually threats that humans can remove.
When a species is declining because of overhunting or habitat loss, the remedy is clear: ban the hunting, protect the forest, and the population often recovers.

By contrast, when a species is fading because of slow natural processes, such as competition with a better-adapted rival, even a large budget may only delay the end, and spending on such cases can be [[futile|futile]].
Medicine offers a parallel: in my work as an epidemiologist, we direct resources first to causes we can modify, such as unsafe water, rather than to risks we cannot change.
Consequently, the policy acts like a triage rule, and in a world of limited funds, triage based on what can be fixed is a [[prudent|prudent]] choice rather than a cold one.
Admittedly, the policy has a serious weakness: in practice, it is often difficult to separate human causes from natural ones.

A frog species may be dying from a fungal disease, which looks natural, yet the fungus may have spread around the world through the human pet trade; likewise, a coral reef may be bleaching because of warming seas that human emissions helped to cause.
Nevertheless, this difficulty argues for a careful definition of human activity, not for abandoning the policy.
If agencies count indirect effects such as introduced diseases and climate change, the rule will cover most of the species now at risk, and the few truly natural declines can be judged case by case.

In other words, the [[ambiguous|ambiguous]] cases [[qualify|qualify]] my support rather than overturn it: the policy is sound only if it is applied with scientific judgment instead of a narrow legal reading.
In conclusion, I support the policy of focusing conservation efforts on species threatened by human activity, provided that the term is defined broadly.
Such a policy matches responsibility to cause, concentrates limited resources on threats that can actually be removed, and can handle unclear cases through sound scientific assessment.
Applied in this way, the policy would not make society [[indifferent|indifferent]] to nature; it would make society accountable for its own impact on nature.

essays.title: Species are worth saving whatever the cause

paragraphs.text: A species that disappears cannot be brought back, whatever the reason it disappeared.
The policy under discussion would nonetheless limit conservation to species whose potential extinction results from human activities.
I largely oppose this policy, because the value of a species does not depend on what threatens it, although I accept that human-caused threats deserve priority when funds are scarce.

Three consequences shape this position: the policy would force agencies into a slow search for causes, it would allow the loss of species whose value we cannot yet foresee, and it is not needed to set sensible priorities.
First, implementing the policy would delay action, because agencies would have to prove the cause of a decline before they could respond.
In ecology, as in epidemiology, causes are rarely simple.
A bird population may shrink because of a disease, a drought and the loss of a few nesting sites all at once, and scientists may argue for years about which factor matters most.
Under this policy, each argument would become a legal question, and while experts debated, the population could fall below the point of recovery.
Similarly, in outbreak response, we do not wait to confirm the exact source of an epidemic before we start protecting people, because delay is the most [[pernicious|pernicious]] error we can make.
This shows that a rule tied to the cause of extinction would [[impede|impede]] the very thing conservation needs most: early, decisive action.
Second, the policy would allow the loss of species that may prove valuable in ways we cannot predict, regardless of why they are declining.
Penicillin offers a clear illustration.
In 1928, Alexander Fleming noticed that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, and that chance observation eventually led to one of the most important drugs in history.
Nature is full of organisms whose useful chemicals or genes remain [[latent|latent]] until someone studies them.
A plant that is disappearing because of a natural change in rainfall may hold a compound as useful as the one in Fleming's mold, but under the proposed policy, no one would be obliged to save it.
Thus, the policy asks the wrong question: what matters is not who caused the threat, but what society would lose if the species were gone.
Admittedly, supporters of the policy make a strong point: resources for conservation are limited, and humans have a special duty to repair the damage they themselves have done.
When logging or poaching drives an animal toward extinction, society clearly owes that species a response, and such threats are also easier to remove than natural ones.
Nevertheless, this argument supports giving human-caused cases priority, not making them the only cases that count.
A hospital, for instance, treats the most urgent patients first, but it does not refuse care to others simply because their illness was not caused by an accident.

In the same way, a [[judicious|judicious]] conservation policy can rank species by urgency, cost and cause without declaring any species unworthy of help, so the consequence I fear is not prioritization but exclusion.
In conclusion, I oppose a rule that limits conservation strictly to species endangered by human activity, although human causes may reasonably come first.
Such a rule would slow responses while causes are debated, would risk the loss of species with unknown value, and is not needed to set sensible priorities.
Society should try to prevent every extinction it can prevent, whatever the cause, and let responsibility shape the order of action rather than its limits.

essays.title: Job prospects deserve a central role

paragraphs.text: For many young people, choosing a major is the first large financial decision of their lives.
Because university education costs years of time and often large debts, some argue that college students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as job availability is treated as the main factor in the choice rather than the only one.

Job prospects matter because they protect students from financial hardship and because they connect education to the needs of society, and the strongest objection, that passion drives success, can be met within this approach.
First, students should weigh job availability heavily because a degree without a job market can leave them in a [[precarious|precarious]] position for years.
In Vietnam, many families borrow money or sell land to send a child to university in Hanoi or Ho Chi Minh City.
When that graduate studies a field with few openings, the family's sacrifice may produce years of underemployment instead of security.
By contrast, a graduate in a field with many openings can usually start earning, repay the family and build a career.
Similarly, a graduate with heavy student loans in the United States has little freedom to wait for an ideal job; the debt requires an income now.
This shows that job availability is not a shallow concern; for most students, it determines whether education becomes a path out of hardship or a new source of it.
Moreover, choosing fields with strong demand helps society as well as the individual, since job openings often signal unmet social needs.
Consider a country facing a shortage of doctors and nurses in rural districts.
When students respond to that demand by entering the health professions, they gain stable careers, and patients in underserved areas finally receive care.
In my own field, the demand for epidemiologists grew sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic, and those trained in data analysis could [[alleviate|alleviate]] a real public problem.
Likewise, once GPS was opened to civilians, it became the basis of ride-hailing and delivery apps, and students who studied software engineering helped build services that millions now use.
Thus, when students let the labor market guide them, they are not merely protecting themselves; they are directing their talent to where society needs it most.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that passion and ability, not job counts, are what lead people to excel.

Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history; had he chosen a career by market demand, the world would have lost his work.
Nevertheless, such cases are rare, and most students are not choosing between greatness and a paycheck but between a stable career and an uncertain one.
Moreover, interest and demand often overlap: a student who loves art can study design, and one who loves biology can enter public health.

This challenge therefore refines my position rather than [[refuting|refute]] it: job availability should lead the decision, but students should look for the in-demand field that best fits their interests.
In conclusion, I largely agree that college students should base their choice of field mainly on the availability of jobs.
Doing so protects them from financial insecurity and directs their skills toward society's needs, and it need not crush personal interest if students choose wisely within growing fields.
The wisest choice is rarely passion alone or demand alone, but a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] match between the two, with demand setting the boundaries.

essays.title: Job markets are too unstable to guide majors

paragraphs.text: Few things change faster than the labor market.
Even so, some argue that college students should base their choice of a field of study on the availability of jobs in that field.
I mostly disagree with this claim: job availability deserves some weight, but it should not be the basis of the choice, because aptitude and interest predict long-term success more reliably.

Job forecasts are unreliable over the length of a career, students who study what engages them tend to perform and adapt better, and the strongest counterargument, financial risk, calls for planning rather than surrender.
First, basing a major on job availability is risky because today's demand may not survive four years of study, let alone a forty-year career.
Kodak illustrates how quickly a secure field can collapse.
Its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
A student who had chosen a career in film photography because jobs were plentiful would have found that security [[ephemeral|ephemeral]].
Conversely, once GPS was opened to civilians, it created whole industries, such as ride-hailing and delivery apps, that few students could have planned for.
This shows that job availability is a moving target, so a choice based on it alone is often a [[myopic|myopic]] bet on the present.
Choosing a field because it offers many jobs today is like buying a house because it is fashionable this year: the value may not last.
Second, students who follow genuine interest and ability are more likely to excel and to adapt, and those qualities matter more than the size of a field.

The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
No job market existed for aviators at the time; their curiosity created one.
In medicine, too, I have noticed that colleagues who chose their specialty out of interest are often more [[assiduous|assiduous]] in research than those who chose the most profitable option.
Thus, interest is not a luxury but a source of the persistence that long careers require, and persistence is what turns a degree into a career.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my view is financial: many students cannot afford to graduate without work.
In Vietnam, where families often sacrifice heavily to pay tuition, a graduate in a crowded field may face years of unemployment, and that burden falls on parents as well as on the student.
Nevertheless, this risk is better managed through planning than by letting job counts decide everything.
A student who loves history can add data or language skills, and a student drawn to biology can specialize in public health, where jobs are more plentiful.

In this way, students can [[mitigate|mitigate]] financial risk while keeping interest at the center of the decision, which is why the challenge [[qualifies|qualify]] my position but does not reverse it.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that job availability should be the basis for choosing a field of study.
Job markets shift too quickly to forecast, interest and aptitude drive the effort that success demands, and financial concerns can be addressed without abandoning those strengths.
Students should therefore treat the job market as a guide to how they prepare, not as a command about what they must study.

essays.title: Each answer opens deeper questions

paragraphs.text: Every scientist knows the experience of answering one question only to find three new ones behind it.
This experience lies behind the statement that as we acquire more knowledge, things do not become more comprehensible, but more complex and mysterious.
I largely agree with this statement, at least at the frontier of research, although I accept that knowledge makes many practical problems far easier to understand.
Knowledge reveals hidden complexity in nature, it exposes the limits of earlier certainties, and, while it does simplify everyday problems, it rarely makes the world as a whole simpler.
First, I agree because each advance tends to uncover layers of complexity that earlier thinkers could not see.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Many expected that the sequence would explain most diseases.
Instead, scientists found that genes interact with one another and with the environment in ways far more [[convoluted|convoluted]] than a simple code.
Similarly, in my work on dengue, each new study of the virus and its mosquito hosts has revealed more variables, such as climate, household water storage and human movement, rather than fewer.
This shows that knowledge often turns a seemingly simple question into a web of related questions, just as the statement suggests.
Each answer, in other words, raised a larger set of questions than the one it settled.
Moreover, new knowledge frequently reveals that what we thought we understood was incomplete or wrong.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Findings that once seemed settled suddenly became uncertain, and the field became more aware of how much it did not know.

Likewise, penicillin seemed to solve bacterial infection, yet Alexander Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse would breed resistant bacteria, and resistance is now an [[intractable|intractable]] global problem.
Therefore, knowledge does not simply add to understanding; it often [[undermines|undermine]] confident beliefs and replaces them with deeper uncertainty.
A field that once seemed close to final answers now has to rebuild its foundations, which is exactly the kind of growing complexity the statement describes.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true for many practical problems, where knowledge clearly makes things more comprehensible.

Childbed fever was once a deadly [[enigma|enigma]], and when Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that handwashing reduced deaths on his ward, most colleagues rejected his idea; germ theory later explained why he was right.
Nevertheless, solving such problems usually moves the mystery rather than removing it.
Germ theory answered the question of what causes infection, but it opened new questions about immunity, resistance and the behavior of microbes that researchers are still studying.
Indeed, the more microbiologists learn, the more they find that many microbes in our bodies are helpful rather than harmful, a discovery that makes the picture richer and harder to summarize.
Thus, knowledge makes particular problems clearer while making the larger picture more complex, so this consideration limits my agreement to the frontier of research rather than reversing it.
In conclusion, I largely agree that greater knowledge tends to make the world appear more complex and mysterious, especially at the edge of what we know.
New discoveries reveal hidden layers, overturn earlier certainties, and, even when they clarify practical problems, raise new questions in their place.
This is not a reason for despair but for humility: the more we know, the more [[keenly|keen]] we should recognize what we do not.

essays.title: Knowledge makes the world more understandable

paragraphs.text: A child who hears thunder may fear an angry god; an adult who understands electricity hears only a storm.
This contrast challenges the statement that as we acquire more knowledge, things do not become more comprehensible, but more complex and mysterious.
I mostly disagree with this statement: although new knowledge often reveals fresh questions, its main effect is to make the world more comprehensible and easier to act upon.

Knowledge explains phenomena that once seemed mysterious, it allows us to solve problems that were once unsolvable, and the new complexity it reveals is usually a sign of deeper understanding rather than greater mystery.
First, knowledge makes things more comprehensible because it replaces mystery with explanation.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most colleagues [[dismissed|dismiss]] his idea, partly because no accepted theory explained why it worked.
Only when germ theory vindicated him, years after his death, did the result make sense: microbes carried on unwashed hands caused the disease.
Similarly, the Church forced Galileo in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, but today any schoolchild understands that it does.
These cases show that knowledge does not deepen mystery; it turns what was once [[arcane|arcane]] into common understanding.
What frightened or confused earlier generations has become, through knowledge, a matter of simple explanation.
Second, knowledge makes the world more comprehensible in the most practical sense: it lets us predict and control events.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
That success was possible only because scientists had [[elucidated|elucidate]] how the virus spread and how vaccines protected people.

Likewise, knowing that Wolbachia bacteria block dengue transmission allowed researchers to release mosquitoes carrying them, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
In my own work on dengue, better knowledge of where mosquitoes breed has made outbreaks easier, not harder, to predict and prevent.
If knowledge only made things more mysterious, such [[efficacious|efficacious]] interventions could not exist; the fact that they work shows that we understand more than we once did.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in one important sense: every answer at the frontier of science tends to raise new questions.
The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, gave researchers the full human DNA sequence, yet it also revealed that genes interact with one another and with the environment in very complex ways.
Nevertheless, recognizing complexity is itself a form of understanding, not a return to mystery.
Before the genome was sequenced, scientists did not know what they did not know; now they can name specific questions and design studies to answer them.
Researchers now study gene interactions with clear methods, and each study narrows the unknown a little further.

In short, knowledge exchanges vague mysteries for precise problems, and a precise problem is far more comprehensible than a vague one, which is why this point refines my position without overturning it.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that knowledge makes things more complex and mysterious rather than more comprehensible.
Knowledge explains what once seemed inexplicable, allows us to prevent disease and solve practical problems, and even the complexity it uncovers is a sign of progress.
Our questions grow more detailed as we learn, but that is because we finally understand enough to ask them.

essays.title: Disagreement is the engine of progress

paragraphs.text: Groups of like-minded people often feel efficient, but agreement can hide mistakes that no one is willing to name.
This danger supports the statement that in any situation, progress requires discussion among people who have contrasting points of view.
I largely agree with this statement, although "in any situation" is too strong, since emergencies sometimes call for quick decisions rather than debate.
Contrasting views expose errors, they produce better decisions in leadership and business, and the limits of debate in a crisis show where the statement needs qualification.
First, discussion among people who disagree is necessary for progress because it exposes errors that a uniform group would miss.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Many original findings had been accepted without enough challenge; once skeptical researchers tested them, the field learned how often single findings mislead.
Similarly, in my own research, the most useful comments on a manuscript usually come from the reviewer who disagrees with my methods, not from the one who praises them.
This shows that progress in knowledge depends on [[dissent|dissent]]: without people willing to question, errors simply accumulate.
A finding that has survived the attacks of its critics is far more trustworthy than one that has only been praised by its friends.
Second, leaders who invite contrasting points of view tend to make wiser decisions than those surrounded by agreement.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Their objections forced him to test his plans against strong arguments, and the result was a government more capable than one built on loyalty alone.
Lincoln did not enjoy their criticism, but he understood that a leader who hears only agreement learns nothing new.

By contrast, Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace the digital camera that its own engineer Steven Sasson had invented in 1975, and it filed for bankruptcy in 2012; a company that took internal critics more seriously might have survived.
These cases suggest that a [[homogeneous|homogeneous]] group may feel comfortable, but it is often [[complacent|complacent]] about risks that a diverse group would catch.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true in every situation, because some moments demand action more than discussion.
When a patient arrives in the emergency room in cardiac arrest, the team follows a fixed protocol; a debate among doctors with contrasting views at that moment could cost a life.
Nevertheless, even in such cases, the protocol itself was the product of earlier debate.
Resuscitation guidelines are revised regularly after experts with different views review new evidence and argue about it.
The speed of the emergency team depends on arguments that took place months earlier, in calmer settings.
Therefore, debate can be postponed in a crisis, but it cannot be removed from the process of progress; this qualifies the words "in any situation" without weakening the core of the statement.
In conclusion, I largely agree that progress depends on discussion among people with contrasting points of view, though not necessarily at every moment.
Such discussion exposes errors, strengthens decisions, and shapes even the rules we follow in emergencies, when debate must wait.
The lesson for any team or institution is to make room for [[candid|candid]] disagreement before decisions are made, so that action can be swift when it is needed.

essays.title: Progress often comes without debate

paragraphs.text: Debate is often praised as the engine of progress, yet many breakthroughs began with a single person or a small team working quietly.
This tension calls into question the statement that in any situation, progress requires discussion among people who have contrasting points of view.
I mostly disagree with this statement: such discussion is often helpful, but it is not required for progress, and in some situations it can even slow progress down.
Many advances come from focused individuals or small teams, debate can delay urgent action, and although contrasting views are valuable for testing ideas, they are only one path to progress.
First, the statement does not hold true for many advances, which come from individuals or small, like-minded teams rather than from debate.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Their progress came from patient testing, not from arguments with experts who held opposing views.
When experts later doubted their claims, the brothers answered with public demonstrations rather than with debate.

Similarly, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, and her success rested on [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] laboratory work rather than public debate.
These cases show that progress often depends on persistence and evidence; discussion with opponents may come later, but it is not what produces the breakthrough.
Second, when action is urgent, prolonged discussion among people with contrasting views can actually [[impede|impede]] progress.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
If the government had waited until every group, including riders who found helmets hot or inconvenient, reached agreement, many more people might have died while the debate continued.
Likewise, during an outbreak, public health teams must often act on the best available evidence rather than wait for every doubting expert to be persuaded.
In such situations, progress requires a decision, and endless debate can become a way of avoiding one.
Debate is valuable before a decision, but when lives are at stake, waiting for full agreement is itself a choice with serious costs.
Admittedly, discussion among people with contrasting views is valuable in many situations, especially when ideas need to be tested.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers, and their disagreements helped him avoid mistakes.
Nevertheless, this shows that debate can improve decisions, not that progress is impossible without it.
Even Lincoln, after hearing his critics, had to make final choices himself, and the progress came from those choices.
Had he waited for his rivals to agree with one another, the government might have been paralyzed during a war that demanded quick decisions.

Thus, contrasting views are a useful tool, but the claim that they are required "in any situation" is [[hyperbole|hyperbole]] that ignores how often progress begins with an [[intrepid|intrepid]] individual or a decisive act.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that progress always requires discussion among people with contrasting points of view.
Many breakthroughs come from determined individuals, urgent problems often demand action before agreement, and debate, though useful, is one tool among several.
The wiser principle is to seek contrasting views when there is time to test ideas, but not to make progress wait for them.

essays.title: Honest guidance protects students' futures

paragraphs.text: Good teachers do more than teach; they also tell students the truth about their prospects.
In this spirit, some argue that educational institutions should dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.
I largely support this policy, provided that "dissuade" means honest advice based on evidence rather than a ban on a student's choice.
Such guidance would save students time and money, it would help them find fields where their strengths can flourish, and its main risk, misjudging talent, can be reduced through careful design.
First, implementing this policy would protect students from costly failure, especially in demanding programs.
Consider medical school in Vietnam, which takes six years and often requires a family's savings.
A student who repeatedly fails basic science courses may continue for years, only to fail the final examinations and leave with no degree.
An adviser who speaks [[candidly|candid]] after the first year could spare that student and family a great deal of hardship.
Similarly, a student who has failed calculus several times may be wise to move from engineering to a field such as business, where quantitative demands are lower.
This shows that well-timed dissuasion is not cruelty; it can [[forestall|forestall]] years of wasted effort and debt.
Honest advice given early is far kinder than a failure discovered late.
Second, steering students away from fields where they are unlikely to succeed can help them discover fields where they will.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and makes teaching a respected and selective profession.
Because entry is selective, applicants who are poorly suited to teaching are directed elsewhere early, and those who remain are well prepared for the work.

In my own experience, several medical classmates who struggled with clinical work found that their real strength lay in research or data analysis, and they thrived once advisers encouraged the change.
Thus, the policy can redirect energy rather than waste it, so that a student's ability is matched to a field in which success is [[feasible|feasible]].
Success in a well-matched field also builds the confidence that students need for the rest of their careers.
Admittedly, the policy carries a serious risk: predictions about who will succeed are often wrong.
The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, would hardly have seemed likely to succeed in aviation, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Similarly, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Nevertheless, this risk argues for careful dissuasion, not for silence.
Institutions can base their advice on several semesters of performance rather than a single test, explain the evidence to the student, and leave the final decision in the student's hands.

Designed in this way, the policy offers honest information without crushing the [[audacious|audacious]] few who can defy the odds, so this consequence shapes how I would implement the policy rather than whether I support it.
In conclusion, I largely support the policy of dissuading students from fields in which they are unlikely to succeed, as long as it takes the form of honest, evidence-based advice.
Such guidance can spare students wasted years, direct them toward fields that fit their strengths, and, when designed with care, avoid discouraging those with unusual talent.
An institution that tells students the truth gently and early serves them better than one that lets them fail quietly.

essays.title: Institutions should inform, not discourage

paragraphs.text: Many people who later excelled in their fields were once told that they had little chance of success.
Even so, some argue that educational institutions should dissuade students from pursuing fields of study in which they are unlikely to succeed.

I largely oppose this policy, because institutions cannot reliably predict success and discouragement can harm the very students it aims to protect, although honest information about difficulty remains useful.
Predictions of success are often wrong, dissuasion would fall most heavily on disadvantaged students, and while frank advice has value, it should inform students rather than steer them away.
First, implementing this policy would rest on predictions that are frequently mistaken.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
Had an art school judged him by his early sales, it might well have advised him to choose another career.
Similarly, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, would hardly have been encouraged to study flight, yet they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
These examples show that "unlikely to succeed" is often a judgment made too early, and a policy built on such judgments would [[squelch|squelch]] talent that has not yet appeared.
An institution that turned such people away would not prevent failure; it would prevent achievement.
Second, the policy would likely [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] existing inequalities, because students from poor or marginalized groups often look less promising on paper.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
In her era, many institutions would have judged a woman unlikely to succeed in physics, not because of her ability, but because of [[ingrained|ingrained]] prejudice.
Today, a student from a rural Vietnamese school with few laboratories may score lower in science than a city student, yet that gap often reflects resources rather than potential.
If advisers judged that student by test scores alone, they would discourage exactly the kind of student whom education is meant to lift.
Thus, dissuasion would tend to send privileged students forward and turn disadvantaged ones away, which is the opposite of what education should do.
Admittedly, supporters of the policy are right that some students waste years and money in programs they cannot complete.
A student who repeatedly fails core courses in a six-year medical program may leave with debt and no degree, and earlier advice might have spared that loss.
Nevertheless, this problem calls for better information and support, not for a policy of discouragement.
Institutions can share completion rates, offer tutoring, and help struggling students consider related fields, while leaving the final choice to them.
A student who receives clear information is still free to try, and many will rise to the challenge.

This consequence therefore shapes my position: I support honest advising, but I reject an official duty to dissuade, because the line between informing and discouraging is easily crossed, and the damage of discouragement is hard to [[redress|redress]].
In conclusion, I largely oppose a policy that asks educational institutions to dissuade students from fields in which they seem unlikely to succeed.
Such predictions are often wrong, they tend to fall hardest on disadvantaged students, and the real problem of failure can be addressed through information and support instead.
Institutions should tell students how hard a path is, but they should let students decide whether to walk it.

essays.title: Caution suits risky research and tight budgets

paragraphs.text: Public money is limited, and every dollar spent on one project is a dollar unavailable for another.
For this reason, some recommend that governments should not fund any scientific research whose consequences are unclear.

I partly agree with this recommendation: where research carries serious risks or where budgets are tight, governments should favor projects with clear consequences, though a ban on all uncertain research would go too far.

Adopting the recommendation would be advantageous when research could cause grave harm and when poorer health systems must use limited funds carefully, but it would be harmful for basic research, which marks the limit of my agreement.
First, adopting the recommendation would be advantageous in circumstances where the possible consequences of research include severe and irreversible harm.
Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.

Similarly, the Tuskegee syphilis study (1932-1972) withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, and the outrage led to rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
In such circumstances, refusing to support research with unclear and possibly [[deleterious|deleterious]] consequences is not timid; it protects the public that pays for science.
Second, the recommendation would be advantageous where public budgets are small and needs are [[pressing|pressing]].

Consider a provincial health department in Vietnam choosing between an exploratory genetics project with unclear benefits and a study on scaling up Wolbachia mosquitoes, which cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
The second choice offers clearer value to taxpayers and to the families who suffer from dengue every rainy season.

Similarly, a country facing antibiotic resistance, driven by overuse and over-the-counter sales, would act [[prudently|prudent]] by funding studies of prescribing practices before more uncertain projects.
In these circumstances, favoring research with clear consequences is a way of spending scarce funds where they will most likely save lives.
For a poor health system, a clear and modest benefit is often worth more than a large but uncertain promise.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would be clearly disadvantageous for basic research, whose value often appears only decades later.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine; a strict rule against unclear research might have stopped that work long before its value was visible.
Nevertheless, this example shows that the word "any" is too strong, not that caution is wrong.
A sensible system could reserve a fixed share of funding for open-ended research judged by peer review, while applying stricter tests to projects that could cause public harm.
Thus, the mRNA case narrows my agreement rather than [[negating|negate]] it.
In conclusion, I partly agree that governments should avoid funding research with unclear consequences, particularly when that research might cause harm or when funds are scarce.

The thalidomide and Tuskegee cases show the value of caution, and the needs of poorer health systems show the value of clear priorities, yet the history of mRNA vaccines shows that uncertainty is also where discovery begins.
The best policy is therefore not a ban on uncertain research but a balance that keeps risky work under strict review and basic science alive.

essays.title: Uncertain research drives the greatest advances

paragraphs.text: Some of the most useful discoveries in history began as projects whose practical purpose no one could clearly explain.
Nevertheless, some recommend that governments should not fund any scientific research whose consequences are unclear.

I largely disagree with this recommendation, because unclear consequences are a normal feature of valuable research, although governments should apply strict oversight where possible harms are serious.

Funding uncertain research is advantageous when it builds the foundation for future breakthroughs and when private companies will not pay for it, and only in circumstances of clear danger is restraint warranted.
First, rejecting the recommendation would be advantageous for basic research, since its consequences are often unclear for decades.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
When their work began, few could have predicted that it would help the world respond to a pandemic.

Similarly, when Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate, the practical consequences were unclear; penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II.
These cases show that a rule against unclear research would cut off discoveries at their [[nascent|nascent]] stage, long before their value could be seen.
Second, government funding of uncertain research is especially advantageous in circumstances where private companies have little reason to invest.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Its long-term uses were uncertain, and a private company would have had little reason to give such results away, yet the sequence became a shared resource for research worldwide.
Likewise, GPS was built by the US military; once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
Few of the engineers who designed it could have predicted these everyday uses.
Thus, public funding is often the only way uncertain research happens at all, and its benefits [[redound|redound]] to entire societies rather than to a single investor.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would be advantageous, namely when research or new products could seriously harm people.
Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, and Frances Kelsey of the US FDA was right to refuse its approval.
Nevertheless, the lesson of thalidomide is that risky products need careful testing and review, not that uncertain research should go unfunded.
Indeed, the US responded by passing stricter drug-testing rules in 1962, which demanded more research before approval, not less.
The same is true of human research: the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, led to ethics review boards, not to a ban on research.
Therefore, the danger of harm justifies [[exacting|exacting]] oversight, but it does not justify the blanket ban that the recommendation proposes.
In conclusion, I largely disagree that governments should refuse to fund research whose consequences are unclear.
Uncertain research has given us new vaccines, antibiotics and shared tools such as the human genome sequence and GPS, and its real risks can be managed through review rather than avoidance.
A government that funds only what it can predict will [[forfeit|forfeit]] the discoveries it cannot yet imagine.

essays.title: Early training lets talent flourish

paragraphs.text: Many skills, from music to mathematics, are easiest to develop when learners start young.
This fact supports the recommendation that society should identify children who have special talents and provide training for them at an early age.
I largely agree with this recommendation, provided that identification is broad and repeated over time rather than a single test that labels children for life.

Early training is advantageous when skills require long practice and when it helps gifted children from poor families gain opportunities, and it is disadvantageous mainly when programs become narrow and rigid.
First, adopting the recommendation would be advantageous in fields where excellence requires years of practice that must begin in childhood.
Consider a talented young violinist in Hanoi.
If she begins serious training at seven, she can master technique while her hands and mind are most [[malleable|malleable]]; if she starts at seventeen, even great talent may not close the gap.
The same pattern holds in many sports and in languages, where early learners usually reach higher levels.
Similarly, a child who shows unusual skill in mathematics gains far more from advanced material at ten than from repeating lessons she has already mastered.
In such circumstances, early training does not create talent; it gives existing talent the time it needs to develop fully.
Delaying that training would waste years that no later effort can fully recover.
Second, the recommendation would be especially advantageous for gifted children from poor families, who rarely receive special training otherwise.
Wealthy parents can pay for private tutors, music lessons and summer programs, so their children's talents are usually noticed.
A gifted child in a remote village, by contrast, may never be identified unless a public program looks for her, and without such a program, her ability may remain [[dormant|dormant]] for life.
Finland, which makes teaching a respected and selective profession, shows how well-trained teachers can notice individual students' strengths without relying heavily on standardized testing.
This shows that a public effort to find and train talent can make opportunity more [[equitable|equitable]], rather than leaving it to family wealth.
In such circumstances, early identification is not a privilege for the few but a correction of the advantages that wealth already provides.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which the recommendation would not be advantageous, particularly when programs label children too early or push them too hard.
A child selected at six for an elite program may face [[onerous|onerous]] expectations, lose interest in other subjects, and suffer if she later falls behind her peers.
Nevertheless, these problems come from poor design, not from the idea of early training itself.
Programs that assess children repeatedly, allow them to enter or leave at any age, and protect time for play can reduce these harms.
A child who is not selected at six should be able to join at ten, and a child who loses interest should be free to leave without shame.
These risks therefore shape my position: I support early training only when it keeps doors open instead of closing them.
In conclusion, I largely agree that society should identify talented children and train them early, as long as identification is broad and flexible.
Such training is advantageous in skills that demand long practice and for gifted children whose families cannot pay for help, and its risks can be reduced through careful program design.
The goal should be to give every talent a chance to grow, not to decide a child's future before it has begun.

essays.title: Early labels limit more than they help

paragraphs.text: Children change quickly, and the eight-year-old who seems ordinary may become an extraordinary adult.
This unpredictability poses a problem for the recommendation that society should identify children with special talents and train them from an early age.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because early identification is unreliable and may narrow children's lives, although targeted support can be advantageous in a few fields.

Early selection would be disadvantageous because talent is hard to predict and because it would favor already privileged children, and although it may help in fields that demand early practice, broad education serves most children better.
First, adopting the recommendation would be disadvantageous in most circumstances because talent in childhood is a poor predictor of adult achievement.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
A program that searched for artistic talent among young children might easily have missed him, since greatness of his kind is rarely visible in childhood.

Similarly, the Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, and their first powered flight in 1903 came from years of adult experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel, not from early training.
These cases show that talent often appears late and in unexpected forms, so early selection rewards early bloomers and overlooks people whose abilities are still [[latent|latent]].
A system that commits its resources at age seven will inevitably bet on the wrong children.
Second, early identification programs would likely favor children who are already privileged, especially where resources are uneven.
In Vietnam, as in many countries, children in large cities have better schools, private tutors and parents who are [[conversant|conversant]] with how selection tests work.
If talent programs choose children at age seven, city children will fill most places, not because they are more gifted but because they have been better prepared.
Finland offers a contrast: it relies far less on standardized testing than many countries and instead requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, investing in strong teaching for all students.
This shows that early selection can deepen inequality while appearing to reward merit, which is a [[pernicious|pernicious]] outcome for a public program.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which the recommendation would be advantageous, particularly in fields such as music or sports that demand early, intensive practice.
A gifted young pianist or gymnast may lose valuable years if serious training begins only in adolescence.
Nevertheless, such fields are exceptions, and even there, training can be offered to any interested child rather than reserved for a few chosen early.
Open music classes and school sports teams allow talent to reveal itself over time, and coaches can then provide extra support to those who progress.
In this way, children who discover a passion at twelve or fifteen are not excluded simply because they were overlooked at six.
These exceptions [[qualify|qualify]] my position: special training has a place, but early labels and selective tracks should not become the general rule.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that society should identify talented children early and give them special training.
Childhood talent is hard to judge, early selection tends to favor the privileged, and even fields that need early practice are better served by open programs than by narrow selection.
Society would do more for talent by giving every child a strong, broad education and keeping the door to special training open at every age.

essays.title: Groups shape who we become

paragraphs.text: When people introduce themselves, they rarely begin with their private thoughts; they say where they come from, what they do and whom they belong to.
This habit lends support to the statement that it is primarily through our identification with social groups that we define ourselves.
I largely agree with this statement, although some individuals define themselves against the groups that formed them.
Groups supply our values and roles, shared struggle turns group membership into personal identity, and even those who rebel against one group usually define themselves through another.
First, I agree because the groups we belong to give us the values and roles through which we understand ourselves.

In Vietnam, many people describe themselves first as members of a family and a hometown; a young doctor may see her career as a duty to her parents and her community rather than as a purely personal choice.
These group identities are [[ingrained|ingrained]] early, through family meals, festivals and shared expectations.
Similarly, my identity as a physician was shaped less by private reflection than by years among other doctors, whose standards and habits I gradually adopted as my own.
This shows that much of what we call the "self" is learned from the groups around us, just as the statement suggests.
Even the language in which we think about ourselves is a gift from the communities that raised us.
Moreover, shared struggle can turn group membership into the core of personal identity.
During the Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, and the boycott helped end bus segregation in that city.
For many participants, the experience shaped who they were: not isolated victims, but members of a community acting in [[solidarity|solidarity]].
Their courage came not only from private conviction but also from knowing that neighbors, churches and families were taking the same risk together.
Likewise, smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011, and for many young people, belonging to that movement became part of how they saw themselves.
These cases suggest that identification with a group is often the very means by which people discover and express who they are.
In such moments, the line between "who I am" and "who we are" almost disappears.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold true for some individuals, who define themselves largely by breaking away from their group.

Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun, yet he is remembered not as a loyal member of that institution but as a thinker who stood apart from it.
Nevertheless, even such [[iconoclasts|iconoclast]] rarely stand entirely alone.
Galileo's identity as a scientist was shaped by the growing community of people who studied nature through observation, as much as by his conflict with the Church.
Rebels, in other words, usually leave one group in order to join another that better fits their convictions.
This consideration therefore [[qualifies|qualify]] my agreement: people may reject one group, but they usually define themselves through another.
In conclusion, I largely agree that we define ourselves primarily through our identification with social groups.
Groups give us our values and roles, shared struggle makes group membership personal, and even rebels tend to find their identity in a new community.
Understanding this should make us more careful about the groups we join, since in choosing them we are also choosing who we become.

essays.title: Choices, not groups, define the self

paragraphs.text: Two siblings raised in the same family, town and religion can grow into very different adults.
This common observation challenges the statement that it is primarily through our identification with social groups that we define ourselves.
I mostly disagree with this statement: social groups shape the starting point of our identity, but we define ourselves primarily through our own choices, work and values.

People often define themselves by choices that go against their groups, our work and commitments matter more than our memberships, and although groups clearly influence us, that influence is a beginning rather than a definition.
First, the statement does not hold true for the many people who define themselves by choices that depart from their groups.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.

Yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea, and he defined himself by his [[principled|principled]] conviction rather than by the profession around him; germ theory vindicated him only years after his death.

Similarly, Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve thalidomide, even though the sedative was already given to pregnant women in Europe, where it caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies.
These cases show that a person's identity is often defined most clearly at the moment when she refuses to [[acquiesce|acquiesce]] to the group.
Second, people define themselves primarily through what they do and value, not through the categories they belong to.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
Had she defined herself by the expectations attached to her gender, she might never have entered science; instead, her identity rested on her [[indefatigable|indefatigable]] work.
In my own life, I share nationality, profession and language with many colleagues, yet I locate my identity in the particular problems I choose to study and the way I approach them.
Thus, group membership tells us what a person has in common with others, while choices and commitments tell us what makes that person an individual.
Two physicians from the same hospital may share a group, yet their choices make them very different people.
Admittedly, the statement holds true in an important sense: groups shape our language, values and early sense of self.
My own habits of speech, my sense of politeness and even my food preferences came from my family and hometown long before I chose a profession.
A child raised in a Vietnamese family learns respect for elders and a sense of duty to relatives long before she can choose any values of her own.
Nevertheless, this early influence is a starting point that adults constantly revise.
Many young Vietnamese, though [[steeped|steeped]] in family loyalty, choose careers, partners and beliefs that their parents never imagined.
These choices, rather than the groups they were born into, are what their friends and colleagues come to know them by.
Therefore, groups provide the raw material of identity, but individuals shape it, which is why I accept the influence of groups while rejecting the word "primarily."
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that we define ourselves primarily through our identification with social groups.
People often reveal who they are by departing from their groups, define themselves through their work and commitments, and treat group influence as a starting point rather than a final answer.
Groups may tell us where we come from, but our choices tell us, and others, who we are.

essays.title: Ask students, but keep experts in charge

paragraphs.text: Most people remember at least one class that felt pointless, and one reason is that no one ever asked them what they needed to learn.
This common experience lies behind the recommendation that educators should find out what students want included in the curriculum and then offer it to them.
I largely agree with this recommendation, as long as student wishes are treated as one important input rather than the final word.

Asking students is most advantageous for adult learners who know their own needs and for any class in which interest fuels effort, although it can backfire when essential but difficult subjects are at stake.
First, adopting the recommendation is clearly advantageous in settings where students are adults who understand the demands of their work.
In my work training district doctors in Vietnam, our early courses on antibiotic use followed a fixed textbook outline, and attendance was poor.

When we surveyed the doctors first, they asked for practical cases on treating common infections without laboratory tests, and once we offered those cases, attendance rose and the discussions became far livelier.
Similarly, a company that asks its engineers which software tools they need will spend its training budget more wisely than one that simply guesses.
This shows that when learners already know what their work requires, finding out what they want is not a surrender to taste but a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] route to useful knowledge.
In such settings, the learners' own requests are the best available map of the gaps that a course should fill.
Second, offering students what they want is advantageous because interest is a powerful engine of effort, even among younger learners.
Consider a secondary school whose students find biology dull until a teacher asks them which health problems worry them most.

When the class chooses to study dengue, which affects many of their families each rainy season, the students survey standing water in their own neighborhoods and learn the mosquito's life cycle with real [[zeal|zeal]].
Likewise, a university statistics course that lets students analyze data from their own majors will usually hold their attention better than one that recycles the same textbook examples every year.
This shows that student preferences, when taken seriously, can [[kindle|kindle]] the motivation without which even the best-designed curriculum fails.
A teacher who ignores those preferences may cover every required topic and still leave most students unchanged.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous where students do not yet know what they will need.
Many young students, if asked, would gladly drop algebra or grammar, yet these subjects are the foundation for nearly every later course and career.
They are not foolish; they simply cannot yet see where those subjects lead.
Nevertheless, this risk argues for limits on student choice, not for ignoring students altogether.
A school can keep core subjects compulsory while asking students which topics, projects or examples should be used to teach them, and which electives should be added.
In this way, educators remain the [[arbiters|arbiter]] of what is essential, while students help decide how it is taught, so this circumstance qualifies my agreement rather than reversing it.
In conclusion, educators should listen to what students want and act on it, but they should not hand over the curriculum entirely.
Student input is most advantageous for adult learners with clear goals and for classes in which interest drives effort, whereas it needs firm limits when essential skills are involved.
The best curriculum, therefore, is built with students rather than simply for them or by them.

essays.title: Curricula should follow needs, not wants

paragraphs.text: Children, if given the choice, would happily eat dessert before every meal.
A similar worry arises from the recommendation that educators should find out what students want included in the curriculum and then offer it to them.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because students' wishes are an unreliable guide to what they actually need, although their input is valuable in limited ways.
Adopting it would be disadvantageous when essential but unpopular subjects are at stake and when popular demand chases passing trends, though it can help in elective and adult courses.
First, adopting the recommendation would be harmful in any setting where the most important subjects are also the least popular.
In Vietnamese medical schools, for instance, many students would happily drop biostatistics and research methods, which seem dry next to clinical work.
Yet in my career as an epidemiologist, those were exactly the skills that allowed me to judge whether a new treatment truly worked or whether a published result was merely a [[fluke|fluke]].

Similarly, when a large collaboration in 2015 tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced only about a third of them, it reminded everyone how much training in sound methods matters.
This shows that students often cannot see the value of a subject until long after they have studied it, so asking them in advance produces a [[myopic|myopic]] curriculum.
A survey of first-year students, in other words, measures their present comfort rather than their future needs.
Second, a curriculum built on student demand would chase fashions that may prove [[ephemeral|ephemeral]].
Consider a university that, responding to a survey, replaces its introductory economics course with a class on building a social media following.
Within a few years the platforms students loved may have changed or disappeared, while the principles of supply, demand and incentives remain as useful as ever.
Likewise, Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace the digital camera its own engineer had invented in 1975 and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

Just as a company that clings to today's demand can miss tomorrow's needs, a school that teaches only what is popular can leave graduates unprepared, which is why educators who can see further ahead should decide.
Students may resent such decisions at first, but most later value the durable skills they were required to learn.
Admittedly, ignoring students entirely would also be a mistake, especially in elective courses and adult education.
A course for working nurses on diabetes care, for example, will be far more useful if the teachers first ask which problems the nurses face on their wards.
Adults with years of practice know their own gaps, and a course that ignores them wastes valuable time.
Nevertheless, such cases involve learners who already have a strong foundation and clear professional goals.
Even for younger students, letting the class choose the novels for one unit can stir interest in reading without removing literature from the program.
In other words, students can [[inform|inform]] the curriculum without controlling it, which limits but does not overturn my position.
Their wishes deserve a voice, but the final decision belongs to those who can see the whole curriculum.
In conclusion, educators should not simply offer students whatever they ask for, even though student views deserve a hearing.
Unpopular subjects are often the most essential, popular demand tends to follow short-lived trends, and student input works best within a structure that experts design.
Educators should therefore consult their students but [[maintain|maintain]] responsibility for what every graduate must know.

essays.title: Concepts first make facts meaningful

paragraphs.text: A list of dates or drug names is easy to forget, but a story that connects them can last a lifetime.
This difference underlies the recommendation that educators should teach facts only after their students have studied the ideas, trends and concepts that help explain those facts.
I largely agree with this recommendation, particularly in subjects where facts are numerous and change over time, although beginners need some basic facts first.

Teaching concepts first is advantageous because it helps students organize and remember facts and because it prepares them for new facts, even though complete beginners need a few facts before any concept makes sense.
First, adopting the recommendation is advantageous in fact-heavy subjects because a concept gives students a framework on which to hang details.
When I studied pharmacology, memorizing dozens of antibiotics one by one was [[arduous|arduous]] and largely [[futile|futile]], since I forgot most names within weeks.
Once a teacher [[elucidated|elucidate]] how bacteria build their cell walls and how each drug class attacks a different step, the same facts became easy to recall because each one had a place.

Similarly, a student who first understands the idea of market incentives can make sense of why Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 turned a country with food shortages into one of the world's largest rice exporters.
This shows that concepts turn scattered facts into a connected system, which is exactly why teaching ideas first is more efficient.
Without the concept, each new fact is one more item to memorize; with it, each fact confirms and enriches an idea.
Second, studying concepts first is advantageous because it prepares students for facts that do not yet exist.
Antibiotic resistance is a clear case: drugs that once cured infections now often fail, so a list of effective drugs memorized by a medical student today may be [[obsolete|obsolete]] within a decade.
A physician who understands natural selection, however, can predict that overuse will breed resistance, just as Alexander Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture.
Likewise, a programmer who grasps general principles of logic can learn any new language, while one who has memorized commands for a single tool is lost when it changes.
This shows that concepts, unlike isolated facts, transfer to new situations, and preparing students for new situations is the real goal of education.
Facts learned in school will age, but a sound concept keeps paying returns long after graduation.
Admittedly, the recommendation would not be advantageous for complete beginners, who need some facts before ideas mean anything.
A child cannot grasp the concept of a food chain without first knowing that rabbits eat grass and foxes eat rabbits, and a medical student cannot understand disease before learning basic anatomy.
Nevertheless, this objection argues for a short foundation of facts, not for teaching facts in isolation for years.
Good teachers introduce a few key facts, use them to build a concept, and then present the remaining details within that framework.
Thus the word "only" in the recommendation is too strict, but its [[gist|gist]], that ideas should guide the learning of facts, remains sound.
In conclusion, educators are generally wise to teach the ideas and trends that explain facts before asking students to master the facts themselves.
Concepts make facts easier to remember and prepare students for facts that will change, although beginners need a small base of facts to start.
The best sequence, therefore, is a few facts, then the concept, and then the rest of the facts in light of it.

essays.title: Facts should come before concepts

paragraphs.text: No one can admire the shape of a building before its bricks are laid.
Yet the recommendation that educators should teach facts only after students have studied the ideas, trends and concepts that explain them asks students to do something similar.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because in most subjects facts are the raw material from which concepts are built, although concepts can guide learning once a foundation exists.
Teaching facts first is advantageous for beginners and essential for testing ideas against evidence, while a concepts-first approach helps mainly advanced students.
First, insisting on concepts before facts would be disadvantageous for beginners, who have nothing to attach an abstract idea to.
Consider a first-year nursing class asked to study the concept of herd immunity before learning what a vaccine is, how infection spreads, or what smallpox was.

The idea would remain [[opaque|opaque]], but students who first learn that smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a global vaccination campaign can then see why protecting enough people protects everyone.
Similarly, children learn multiplication tables before they study functions, and language learners memorize words before they analyze grammar.
In each case, the abstract idea makes sense only because concrete examples have already been stored in memory.
This shows that for novices, facts are not the end of learning but its starting point, so delaying them makes concepts harder, not easier, to grasp.
Teachers who reverse this order often find that students can repeat a definition without being able to apply it.
Second, teaching concepts first risks producing students who accept ideas without checking them against evidence.
Ignaz Semmelweis offers a warning: in 1847 he had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea, and the [[empirical|empirical]] results in front of them were [[dismissed|dismiss]] because they did not fit what they already believed.
Likewise, a student taught a neat theory of economic trends may ignore data that [[contravene|contravene]] it rather than question the theory.
This shows that students who learn facts first are more likely to treat concepts as hypotheses to be tested, which is the habit of mind good education should build.
Concepts should earn their place by explaining facts, not by excusing students from looking at them.
Admittedly, for advanced students, concepts can make the learning of facts far more efficient.
A resident who already understands how bacteria develop resistance can absorb the details of a new antibiotic quickly, because the concept tells her what to look for.
For her, a lecture that opens with the general mechanism is far more efficient than a list of drug names.
Nevertheless, such students acquired their concepts by first learning many facts in earlier years.
Her framework rests on years of memorized anatomy, microbiology and pharmacology, without which the concept of resistance would mean little.
Thus the recommendation may suit the final stage of education, but as a general rule it reverses the natural order in which understanding [[burgeons|burgeon]].
Before that stage, facts should lead and concepts should follow.
In conclusion, educators should not wait to teach facts until students have studied the concepts that explain them.
Facts give beginners something concrete to build on and keep students honest when theories conflict with evidence, even if concepts later speed up learning for advanced students.
The wiser approach is to move back and forth, letting facts suggest concepts and concepts organize facts.

essays.title: Shared views make learning easier at first

paragraphs.text: Most of us learn our first lessons from parents, teachers and friends who see the world much as we do.

This familiar pattern supports the claim that we can usually learn much more from people whose views we share than from those whose views contradict our own, a claim based on the reason that disagreement can cause stress and inhibit learning.
I partly agree with both the claim and the reason, especially for beginners and for learning practical skills, although disagreement remains valuable at later stages.
Shared assumptions let people build knowledge efficiently, and hostile conflict often does block learning, even though some of the most important lessons come from critics.
First, the claim holds in many settings because people who share a basic framework can build on each other's ideas instead of arguing over first principles.
The Human Genome Project, completed in 2003, was a publicly funded international effort in which researchers shared a common goal and could therefore divide the work and combine their results.
Because they agreed on what mattered, each team could build on the others' findings, and the project made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
Similarly, a junior doctor learns surgery fastest from a mentor who shares her basic approach to patient safety, since every lesson adds to what she already accepts.
If her mentor instead challenged every basic assumption, she would spend her energy defending herself rather than learning to operate.
This shows that agreement on fundamentals often [[facilitates|facilitate]] learning, which supports the claim in many practical situations.
Time that would be spent defending basic assumptions can instead be spent learning new material.
Second, the reason offered for the claim is largely true: disagreement, especially when it is hostile, can create stress that inhibits learning.

In my experience teaching epidemiology, students who were [[berated|berate]] by a [[caustic|caustic]] supervisor for questioning a study design stopped asking questions altogether, and their progress slowed.
When the same students joined a supportive group with similar views, they made [[candid|candid]] comments about their doubts and learned more.
Likewise, online arguments about vaccines often turn into insults, and few participants come away better informed.
In such exchanges, people defend their pride rather than examine the evidence.
This shows that the reason has real force, though it applies mainly to disagreement delivered with hostility rather than to disagreement itself.
A frightened learner, after all, cannot think clearly, however valuable the criticism may be in principle.
Admittedly, the strongest objection to the claim is that many crucial lessons come only from people who contradict us.
Abraham Lincoln appointed political rivals such as William Seward to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Their objections forced him to test his plans against the strongest arguments available.
Nevertheless, Lincoln could learn from his rivals because he already had a firm foundation and the confidence to handle conflict.
A first-year student facing constant contradiction, by contrast, may feel lost rather than enlightened and may stop trying.
Thus disagreement is most useful for experienced learners, which [[qualifies|qualify]] rather than overturns my partial agreement with the claim and its reason.
Beginners first need a secure base, which shared views provide; later, they can turn to critics.
In conclusion, I accept the claim and its reason in part, since people who share our views often help us learn more efficiently and hostile disagreement can hinder learning.
Shared frameworks speed cooperation, stress can inhibit learning, and yet critics remain essential once learners are secure.
The practical lesson is to learn the basics among allies and then seek out thoughtful critics.
