essays.title: Disagreement teaches more than agreement

paragraphs.text: An echo can repeat our words, but it can never teach us anything new.

That is the weakness of the claim that we can usually learn much more from people whose views we share than from those who contradict us, a claim based on the reason that disagreement can cause stress and inhibit learning.
I largely disagree with both the claim and the reason, because disagreement is often the main source of new knowledge, and the stress it causes is usually manageable and even useful.
Contrary views expose our errors, moderate stress can sharpen learning, and only hostile conflict truly inhibits it.
First, the claim is mistaken because people who share our views mostly confirm what we already believe, whereas critics reveal our errors.

When Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime in 1847, deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet colleagues who shared the same assumptions rejected his idea.
Medicine learned the lesson only when germ theory, which contradicted their beliefs, vindicated him years after his death.
Similarly, the 2015 effort that reproduced only about a third of 100 published psychology studies came from researchers willing to question findings their own field accepted.

This shows that groups of like-minded people easily grow [[complacent|complacent]], and that progress often depends on hearing the views we least want to hear, which [[undermines|undermine]] the claim.
A community that hears only agreement has no way to discover what it has gotten wrong.
Second, the reason is only partly true, and even where it is true, it does not support the claim.

Disagreement can certainly cause stress, but moderate stress often focuses attention; a young doctor who must defend her diagnosis to a [[skeptic|skeptic]] on the ward examines the evidence more carefully than one whose colleagues simply nod.
In my own research, the reviewer comments that stung most also improved my papers most.
Likewise, Abraham Lincoln chose able critics such as William Seward for his cabinet rather than loyal followers.
He accepted friction within his own government as the price of hearing objections that loyal followers would never raise.
This shows that the discomfort of disagreement is often a sign that learning is happening, not that it is being blocked.
Stress, in other words, is not always the enemy of learning; often it is the feeling of an old belief being tested.
Admittedly, the most compelling support for the reason is that hostile, personal disagreement can make people defensive and stop them from learning at all.
On social media, where misinformation spreads faster than corrections can follow, angry debates often [[polarize|polarize]] users rather than inform them.
In these settings, users often leave an argument more certain of their original views than before.
Nevertheless, the problem in such cases is the manner of the disagreement, not the fact of it.
When critics argue respectfully, as in a well-run journal club where colleagues test each other's interpretations, contrary views teach far more than polite agreement.
Thus the stress the reason describes calls for better ways of disagreeing rather than for retreating to people who think as we do.
Even if hostile disagreement inhibits learning, the claim does not follow, because respectful disagreement remains the richest source of new ideas.
In conclusion, we usually learn more from people who challenge our views than from those who share them.
Critics reveal errors that allies miss, moderate stress sharpens rather than blocks thinking, and the harm of hostile conflict can be reduced by civility.
The wise learner, therefore, seeks out disagreement instead of avoiding it.

essays.title: Officials should judge, not simply obey

paragraphs.text: A doctor who prescribed whatever patients demanded would soon do more harm than good.
A similar logic applies to the recommendation that government officials should rely on their own judgment rather than unquestioningly carry out the will of the people they serve.
I largely agree with this recommendation, especially when officials have expert knowledge that the public lacks, provided that they explain their decisions and remain accountable.
Independent judgment is advantageous when experts understand hidden risks and when a majority would harm a minority, but it becomes dangerous when officials stop listening to citizens.
First, relying on judgment is advantageous in situations where experts understand risks that the public cannot easily see.
Around 1960, thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the United States then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Had she treated approval as a formality, many American families might have suffered the same tragedy.
Similarly, Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets was not welcomed by every rider, yet it raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
This shows that blind [[deference|deference]] to public demand can cost lives, while officials who use informed judgment can save them.
In such circumstances, the public interest is served precisely when officials refuse to treat popularity as proof of safety.
Second, independent judgment is advantageous when the majority's will would harm a minority.
In Montgomery in the 1950s, segregated buses reflected the wishes of the local majority, and Black residents had to refuse for over a year to ride them before bus segregation ended in that city.
An official who unquestioningly carried out the majority's will would simply have defended that [[iniquity|iniquity]].
Likewise, a health official in a town where most residents oppose a clinic for HIV patients should still open it, because those patients have an equal right to care.
Fear of a disease does not give neighbors the right to deny care to patients.
This shows that the will of the people is not always the will of all the people, and judgment is needed to protect those who are outvoted.
Majorities can be wrong about the rights of others, and officials swear to serve everyone, not merely the largest group.
Admittedly, adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous when officials [[arrogate|arrogate]] to themselves decisions that belong to citizens.
A mayor who builds an expensive highway through a neighborhood whose residents wanted a park may claim superior wisdom while simply serving powerful interests.
Residents would rightly see such a decision as arrogance rather than leadership.
Nevertheless, the remedy for such abuse is accountability, not obedience.
Elections, a free press and public explanation of decisions allow citizens to check officials without dictating every choice.
An official who must defend each major decision in public is far less likely to confuse personal interest with sound judgment.
Thus the danger of arrogant officials qualifies my position: judgment should be independent but never [[covert|covert]], so that citizens can see and challenge the reasons behind it.
In conclusion, government officials should generally rely on their own judgment rather than simply follow public demands.
Expert judgment prevents harm when risks are hidden and protects minorities from the majority, although it must stay open to scrutiny so that it does not become arrogance.
The best officials, therefore, listen carefully to the people but decide according to evidence and principle.

essays.title: Officials should usually follow the people

paragraphs.text: In a democracy, power is lent to officials, not given to them.
That principle is challenged by the recommendation that government officials should rely on their own judgment rather than unquestioningly carry out the will of the people they serve.

I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because officials who override the public too readily make costly mistakes and lose trust, although expert judgment is needed when lives are clearly at stake.

Following the people's will is advantageous because citizens often know local conditions better and because policies they support are more likely to succeed, even if officials must occasionally lead against opinion.
First, carrying out the people's will is advantageous in settings where citizens understand local needs better than distant officials.
Before 1986, Vietnam relied on central planning, in which officials rather than farmers decided how the economy should work, and the country faced food shortages.

The Doi Moi reforms replaced central planning with market incentives that let people act on their own choices, and Vietnam became one of the world's largest rice exporters as poverty fell dramatically.
Similarly, in dengue control I have seen campaigns designed without community input fail because they ignored how residents actually store water.
Residents knew which containers mattered and which did not, and plans that respected that knowledge worked far better.
This shows that the people's will often carries knowledge that officials lack, so overriding it is rarely as [[sagacious|sagacious]] as it appears.
Officials who claim superior judgment often have less information about daily life, not more.
Second, following the public's will is advantageous because policies that people support are far easier to carry out.
Releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, but such releases take place in people's own neighborhoods.
Officials who imposed them on unwilling communities would invite resistance that could [[stymie|stymie]] even a proven intervention.
Community acceptance, rather than official judgment alone, is what allows a sound intervention to reach the people it is meant to protect.
Likewise, the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, and the public outrage forced new rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.

This shows that officials who ignore the people they serve risk losing the trust on which every public program depends, whereas those who [[accede|accede]] to reasonable public wishes gain cooperation.
A policy that is correct on paper but rejected in practice protects no one.
Admittedly, there are cases, especially when lives are at stake, in which officials must act against popular opinion.
Vietnam's 2007 helmet law was not universally welcomed by riders, yet it raised helmet use to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Nevertheless, such cases are exceptions that require strong evidence, and an official who claims special knowledge should be able to show it publicly.
Without that requirement, any leader could describe an unpopular personal preference as expert judgment.
History offers many leaders who justified unpopular and harmful policies by claiming to know better than the people.
Thus independent judgment should be a rare, [[circumscribed|circumscribe]] power rather than the normal way of governing.
Even then, officials should explain their reasons openly and remain answerable to the public for the results.
In conclusion, officials should usually carry out the will of the people they serve rather than substitute their own judgment.
Citizens often understand local conditions better, and policies with public support are far more likely to succeed, even though rare cases of clear danger justify leading against opinion.
Officials should therefore treat overriding the public as an exception to be justified, never as a habit.

essays.title: Long-term goals outlast quick fame

paragraphs.text: Social media has made it possible to become famous overnight and to be forgotten just as quickly.
In this climate, the recommendation that young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than seek immediate fame and recognition is more relevant than ever.
I largely agree with this recommendation, as long as it is not taken to mean that young people should reject every form of early recognition.
Long-term goals are advantageous because lasting achievement requires sustained effort and because fame-seeking distorts choices, although some young people benefit from early recognition.
First, encouraging long-term goals is advantageous because most valuable achievements require years of patient work.

Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on basic research on mRNA that attracted little notice, yet that work allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year and earned them the 2023 Nobel Prize.
Had they chased quick recognition, they would likely have abandoned such an unfashionable field long before it paid off.
Similarly, the Wright brothers spent years on careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves before their first powered flight in 1903.
They were bicycle makers without college degrees, and no one was applauding their slow, repetitive work.
This shows that [[assiduous|assiduous]] effort toward a distant goal, not a hunt for applause, produces work of lasting value.
Recognition, when it came, was the result of their patience rather than its goal.
Second, the recommendation is advantageous because the pursuit of immediate fame tends to distort young people's choices.
Consider a talented student who could become a public health researcher but instead spends her late teens chasing followers with ever more [[lurid|lurid]] videos.
When the attention fades, as it usually does, she may find herself without skills, qualifications or a clear path.
Her peers who spent those years studying, meanwhile, will have built careers that do not depend on the next viral post.

Likewise, a junior scientist eager for headlines may rush out a striking but weak study, and the 2015 effort that reproduced only about a third of 100 psychology studies shows how often single findings mislead.
This shows that fame is [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] and that chasing it can [[undermine|undermine]] the very work that would bring lasting respect.
A realistic, long-term goal, by contrast, gives young people a reason to build skills that remain valuable after the spotlight moves on.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which early recognition is advantageous, especially in fields such as music or sports where careers begin early.
A teenage athlete who wins a national title may gain sponsors and coaching that would otherwise be out of reach.
For such a young person, refusing all recognition in the name of long-term goals would mean losing real opportunities.
Nevertheless, such recognition is valuable only when it serves a longer goal rather than replacing it.
The athlete who treats a first title as one step in a long career is likely to last far longer than one who treats it as the [[zenith|zenith]] of success.
This exception therefore refines rather than overturns my position, since recognition is welcome as a by-product of long-term goals but not as a goal in itself.
Even the most talented athletes need a plan for the years after their competitive careers end.
In conclusion, young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term goals rather than immediate fame.
Lasting achievements require years of work, and fame-seeking distorts choices, although early recognition can help when it serves a longer plan.
The best advice, then, is to aim high, plan realistically, work patiently and let recognition follow.

essays.title: Bold goals and recognition deserve encouragement

paragraphs.text: Many of the people we now admire were once told that their goals were unrealistic.
That history should make us cautious about the recommendation that young people should be encouraged to pursue long-term, realistic goals rather than seek immediate fame and recognition.

I partly disagree with this recommendation, because its emphasis on "realistic" goals can discourage bold ambition and because early recognition often helps young people succeed, although fame for its own sake is a poor goal.
Seemingly unrealistic dreams have driven major achievements, early recognition can open doors, and only empty fame-seeking deserves discouragement.
First, encouraging only realistic goals would be disadvantageous for young people with unusual talents or ambitions.
The Wright brothers were bicycle makers without college degrees, and powered flight must have seemed an unrealistic goal for such men.
Yet after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves, they achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903.
Similarly, Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, barriers that made her ambitions look far from realistic.
Had the Wright brothers or Curie been encouraged only toward realistic goals, they might have chosen safer, more ordinary careers.
This shows that advice to be "realistic" can [[squelch|squelch]] exactly the ambition that produces breakthroughs.
For a gifted young person, the most realistic goal is sometimes the one that seems unrealistic to everyone else.
Second, seeking early recognition is advantageous in circumstances where visibility creates opportunity.
Consider a young Vietnamese researcher who presents her dengue study at an international conference while still a student.
The recognition she gains may bring a scholarship, a mentor and funding that a quieter path would take a decade to produce.
Without such early visibility, talented students from modest backgrounds may never be noticed by the people who could help them.
By contrast, Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, and his [[posthumous|posthumous]] fame, though enormous, could not support the artist while he lived.
This shows that recognition is not merely vanity, since it is often the [[catalyst|catalyst]] that turns talent into a sustainable career.
Encouraging young people to avoid it entirely would remove one of the main ladders by which talent rises.
Admittedly, the recommendation is right that fame pursued for its own sake is a poor goal.
Young people who chase online popularity with [[meretricious|meretricious]] stunts often gain attention that vanishes within weeks and leaves them with nothing of value.
The recommendation is a useful warning against this kind of empty attention.
Nevertheless, the remedy is to encourage meaningful recognition, not to discourage recognition altogether.
A student who hopes to win a science fair or publish an article is seeking recognition, yet this is a healthy motive that rewards real work.
Such recognition often encourages further effort and attracts the support needed for long-term success.
Thus the recommendation rests on a false [[dichotomy|dichotomy]] between long-term goals and recognition, since the best kind of recognition usually marks progress toward a long-term goal.
Young people should be taught to distinguish fame that rewards real work from fame that replaces it.
In conclusion, I only partly accept the advice that young people should pursue realistic long-term goals instead of immediate recognition.
Bold, seemingly unrealistic goals have produced great achievements, and early recognition often opens doors, even though empty fame is worth little.
Young people should therefore be encouraged to dream boldly and to seek recognition for real accomplishments.

essays.title: Praise teaches better than scolding

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has trained a puppy knows that a reward often works better than a scolding.
Teachers face a similar choice, which is why some recommend that the best way to teach is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones.
I largely agree with this recommendation for minor misbehavior and for young or anxious learners, though serious or dangerous errors cannot be ignored.
Praise builds the confidence and motivation that learners need, and ignoring minor faults denies them the attention they seek, but harmful mistakes require correction.
First, praising positive actions is advantageous because it builds confidence, especially in learners who fear failure.
When I supervised junior health workers collecting dengue data in rural Vietnam, those who were praised for careful records soon became the most [[meticulous|meticulous]] members of the team.
Those who were mainly criticized grew [[timorous|timorous]], hid their errors and asked fewer questions.
Because they feared blame, they also reported problems later, which made the data harder to correct.
Similarly, a primary school teacher who praises a shy child for one correct answer often sees the child raise a hand again the next day.
One small success, noticed and praised, gives the child a reason to risk another attempt.
This shows that praise does more than reward, since it tells learners what to repeat and gives them the courage to try.
Criticism, by contrast, tells learners only what to avoid, and fearful learners often respond by avoiding effort altogether.
Second, ignoring minor negative actions is advantageous in classrooms where misbehavior is a bid for attention.
Consider a student who makes jokes during a lesson to draw a reaction from his classmates.
If the teacher scolds him, he gains the attention he wanted, but if the teacher ignores the jokes and praises him when he contributes seriously, the behavior often [[subsides|subside]].
Likewise, parents who respond calmly to a toddler's tantrum, rather than with anger, often find that the tantrums become less frequent.
The behavior loses its purpose once it no longer produces the reaction it was meant to provoke.
This shows that attention itself is a reward, so ignoring trivial faults can teach as effectively as punishment and without its side effects.
Constant scolding, moreover, can damage the relationship between teacher and student that makes other learning possible.
Admittedly, ignoring negative actions would be harmful when an error is serious or dangerous.
A surgical trainee who fails to wash her hands cannot simply be ignored, because Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand-washing sharply reduced deaths from childbed fever.
A teacher who stayed silent in that situation would be failing both the trainee and her future patients.
Nevertheless, such cases call for clear correction, not for abandoning praise as the main method of teaching.
Even in an operating room, a supervisor can correct a lapse firmly and then praise the trainee when she follows the right procedure.
In this way, the trainee learns the rule without losing the confidence she needs to keep improving.
Thus the recommendation should be [[qualified|qualify]] so that teachers ignore minor faults, correct dangerous ones, and praise generously throughout.
Praise should remain the main tool, while correction is reserved for the errors that truly matter.
In conclusion, praising good actions and ignoring minor bad ones is usually the best way to teach.
Praise builds confidence and shows learners what to repeat, and ignoring attention-seeking behavior removes its reward, although serious errors must be corrected.
A good teacher, therefore, is generous with praise and [[judicious|judicious]] about criticism.

essays.title: Ignoring mistakes leaves learners uninformed

paragraphs.text: A map that showed only the right roads, but never the dead ends, would still leave travelers lost.
This is the problem with the recommendation that the best way to teach is to praise positive actions and ignore negative ones.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because learners need to know what they are doing wrong, although praise should remain a central part of teaching.
Ignoring errors leaves them uncorrected, praise alone can produce [[complacent|complacent]] learners, and only for trivial misbehavior is silence the wise response.
First, ignoring negative actions would be disadvantageous in any field where mistakes have serious consequences for other people.
Antibiotic resistance offers a clear case, since overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread.
As a result, drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
A medical teacher who praised students' correct prescriptions but ignored their unnecessary ones would be helping to create this problem.
Similarly, a driving instructor who ignored a student's failure to check mirrors would be [[abetting|abet]] a future accident.
The student would leave the course confident but dangerous, because no one had ever named the habit that needed to change.
This shows that silence about errors is not neutral, because it lets [[pernicious|pernicious]] habits take root.
Learners cannot fix a mistake that they do not know they are making.
Second, praise without correction is disadvantageous because it can make learners overconfident and unprepared for honest criticism.

In my experience reviewing manuscripts by young researchers, those who had received only encouragement from their supervisors often submitted papers with basic statistical errors and were shocked by reviewers' criticism.
Students who had been given [[candid|candid]] feedback earlier handled peer review far better.
They had learned early that criticism was a normal part of improvement rather than a personal attack.

Likewise, the 2015 finding that only about a third of 100 published psychology studies could be reproduced suggests that a field which rewards striking results without examining weaknesses can mislead itself.
Praise for exciting results is useful only when it is balanced by careful attention to what may be wrong.
This shows that criticism, delivered well, is a form of respect, since it assumes the learner can improve.
Withholding it, however kindly meant, leaves learners to discover their weaknesses later, when the cost is higher.
Admittedly, ignoring negative actions is sensible for minor misbehavior meant to attract attention.
A child who makes noise to provoke the teacher may stop sooner if the noise draws no reaction and quiet work earns praise.
In this narrow case, attention is the reward, and withholding it can change behavior.
Nevertheless, this strategy works only for trivial, attention-seeking behavior, not for errors of understanding or safety.
A student who misunderstands how vaccines work will not correct the error simply because it is ignored; she needs to be shown her mistake patiently rather than [[admonished|admonish]].
Thus the recommendation describes one useful classroom tactic, but it cannot be the best general way to teach.
Praise should remain central, but it must be paired with clear, specific correction whenever an error affects understanding or safety.
In conclusion, praising positive actions while ignoring negative ones is not the best way to teach, even though praise itself is valuable.
Ignored errors persist, praise alone breeds complacency, and only trivial, attention-seeking misbehavior is best met with silence.
The best teachers, therefore, combine generous praise with clear and respectful correction.

essays.title: Worthy goals can justify costly means

paragraphs.text: Few great achievements have come without someone paying a price.
This fact gives some force to the statement that if a goal is worthy, then any means taken to attain it are justifiable.
I agree with this statement to a considerable extent, since worthy goals often justify difficult, unpopular or costly means, although the word "any" goes too far when the means destroy basic rights.

The statement holds when public health measures restrict freedom or demand sacrifice to save lives and when disruptive action ends injustice or hardship, but it fails when the means violate human dignity.
First, the statement holds in public health, where the goal of saving lives justifies measures that limit freedom or demand sacrifice.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets restricted riders' choices, yet it raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Few people today would call that restriction unjustified, because the goal was so clearly worthy.

Similarly, the coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that ended with smallpox being declared eradicated in 1980 relied on countries sharing data and vaccine, setting aside narrow national interests for a common good.
No single country could have achieved that goal alone, and the cooperation it demanded was a price worth paying.
This shows that when a goal is worthy, means that would seem [[onerous|onerous]] in ordinary times become justifiable.
The worthier and more urgent the goal, the heavier the burden that can fairly be imposed to reach it.
Second, the statement holds when a worthy goal requires disrupting an unjust or failing order.
During the Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956, Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, accepting great inconvenience in their own daily lives.
The boycott helped end bus segregation in that city, and its goal of equal treatment clearly justified the hardship.
Those who walked or found other ways to travel for months chose a hard path, but few would now say they were wrong to do so.

Likewise, under Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986, market incentives [[supplanted|supplant]] central planning; the change was sweeping, yet a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters.
This shows that worthy goals can justify means that are costly, disruptive and even [[contentious|contentious]] at the time.
Had the boycotters or the reformers waited for a painless path, the injustice or hardship they faced might have continued for years.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold when the means violate basic human rights.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
No goal could justify deceiving sick men and denying them care.
Nevertheless, this case limits rather than refutes my position, because the problem was that the means destroyed the very dignity medicine exists to protect.
The public outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards, showing that societies accept costly means for worthy goals but draw a firm line at deception and harm.
Thus I accept the statement for means that impose fair costs, but not for means that [[abase|abase]] the people they are supposed to help.
The statement is therefore largely true for costly means but false for cruel ones.
In conclusion, a worthy goal can justify a wide range of difficult means, though not literally any means.
Public health laws and protests against injustice show how worthy aims justify restrictions and disruption, while the Tuskegee study shows where the statement breaks down.
The test, then, is whether the means respect the people they are meant to serve.

essays.task_note: Body 1 and Body 2 show ways the statement holds (public health measures, disruptive protest and reform), and Body 3 shows where it does not hold (rights violations), explaining that this limits the word "any."

essays.title: Noble ends cannot excuse cruel means

paragraphs.text: Many of history's worst abuses were committed by people who believed their goals were good.
That is why the statement that if a goal is worthy, then any means taken to attain it are justifiable is so dangerous.
I strongly disagree with this statement, because unjust means harm real people and often defeat the goal itself, although worthy goals can justify some proportionate costs.
The statement fails when means violate rights and when bad means destroy the trust a goal depends on, and it holds only partly for fair, limited sacrifices.
First, the statement does not hold when the means violate the rights of the people involved.
The Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent in the name of medical knowledge.
Knowledge about disease is a worthy goal, yet no one today would argue that it justified deceiving and harming those men.
The men were treated as sources of data rather than as patients with a right to choose.

Similarly, thalidomide was given to pregnant women around 1960 as a sedative, and it caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe; the hope of helping patients could not excuse giving them a drug before its risks were understood.
This shows that a worthy goal cannot [[exonerate|exonerate]] means that treat people as tools.
The more worthy the goal, in fact, the more carefully we should guard against the temptation to cut corners in pursuing it.
Second, the statement fails because unjust means often [[undermine|undermine]] the very goal they serve.
In my work on dengue control, communities cooperate only when they trust health workers.
A campaign that forced its way into homes to destroy water containers might reduce mosquitoes this season, but it would lose the cooperation needed in every season that follows.
Residents who felt invaded would stop reporting fever cases and hide containers from inspectors.
Likewise, a government that pursued lower crime through torture would teach citizens that the law itself cannot be trusted.
Each forced confession would weaken the very respect for law on which lasting order depends.
This shows that means and ends are linked, because corrupt means [[vitiate|vitiate]] the ends they claim to serve.
A goal reached by unjust means is often not truly reached at all.
Admittedly, the statement holds partly when the means impose fair, limited costs for a clearly worthy goal.
Vietnam's 2007 helmet law restricted riders' freedom, yet it raised helmet use to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Nevertheless, this case shows only that some costly means are justifiable, not that any means are.
The helmet law applied equally to everyone and was [[commensurate|commensurate]] with the danger it addressed.
It did not single out a vulnerable group, deceive anyone or cause harm beyond a small loss of choice.
Thus the real question is never simply whether a goal is worthy but whether the means are proportionate and respectful, which is why I reject the statement as written.
A goal can be worthy and still be pursued in ways that no decent person could accept.
In conclusion, a worthy goal does not make any means justifiable.
Means that violate rights cannot be excused, unjust means tend to defeat their own goals, and even justified sacrifices must be proportionate.
We should judge every plan, therefore, by its methods as well as by its aims.

essays.title: Literature makes better professionals

paragraphs.text: A good novel lets a reader live, for a few hours, inside someone else's mind.

That experience lies behind the recommendation that, in order to become well-rounded individuals, all college students should be required to take courses in which they read poetry, novels, mythology and other imaginative literature.
I largely agree with this recommendation, provided the requirement is modest in size and flexible in content.

Such courses are advantageous because they build empathy in future professionals and because they sharpen the reading and writing skills every field needs, even though they compete for time in demanding programs.
First, requiring literature is advantageous for students entering professions that serve people, because imaginative reading builds empathy.
As a physician, I learned the facts of disease from textbooks, but novels about families coping with illness taught me what a diagnosis feels like to a patient.
That understanding made me more patient with frightened families during dengue outbreaks, when hospitals were crowded and tempers were short.
No statistics table could have given me that insight as vividly as a well-told story did.

Similarly, an engineer designing public housing benefits from stories about how ordinary people live, since a program like Singapore's, which now houses about 80% of residents, must serve real families rather than abstract numbers.
This shows that imaginative literature can [[imbue|imbue]] students with the empathy that well-rounded professionals need.
Professionals who serve people need to understand those people, and fiction offers practice in doing so.
Second, literature courses are advantageous because they sharpen the ability to read closely and write clearly.
Consider a computer science student who must interpret a difficult poem and defend her reading in an essay.
She learns to notice [[nuance|nuance]], weigh evidence and express a complex idea in plain words, skills she will later use in writing reports and explaining her work to clients.
Likewise, many scientists struggle to explain their findings to the public, and close reading of stories could help them make research [[intelligible|intelligible]] to ordinary readers.
Public trust in research depends partly on whether ordinary readers can follow it.
This shows that reading imaginative literature is not a luxury but practical training in thinking and communication.
Even students who never read another poem after graduation will keep the habits of careful reading the course built.
Admittedly, a literature requirement would not be advantageous in programs already crowded with essential technical courses.
A medical or engineering student who must master a heavy load of required subjects may find an extra reading course an [[irksome|irksome]] burden that takes time from clinical or laboratory training.
For such students, a large requirement could mean less practice in the skills their future patients and clients depend on.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for a modest, flexible requirement rather than none at all.
A single course, or a choice among short courses on mythology, poetry or novels, would cost little time while giving every student some exposure.
Students could even choose works connected to their own fields, such as novels about illness for future doctors.
Thus the circumstances of demanding programs shape how the requirement should be designed, not whether it should exist.
A small, well-chosen requirement keeps the benefits of literature while respecting the demands of technical training.
In conclusion, colleges should require all students to read some imaginative literature.
Such courses build empathy and sharpen communication, although the requirement must stay small enough to fit demanding programs.
A modest dose of poetry and fiction, therefore, can produce better professionals and fuller human beings.

essays.task_note: The essay gives circumstances where a literature requirement is advantageous (people-serving professions, communication skills) and one where it is not (crowded technical programs), and explains how that case shapes the design of the requirement.

essays.title: Require breadth, not literature specifically

paragraphs.text: There are many roads to a well-rounded mind.

That is why I question the recommendation that, in order to become well-rounded individuals, all college students should be required to take courses in which they read poetry, novels, mythology and other imaginative literature.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because a single required subject cannot suit every student, although some exposure to the humanities is worthwhile.
A mandatory literature course is disadvantageous when students can gain breadth in other ways and when forced reading breeds resentment, though it can help students who would otherwise never read.
First, the requirement would be disadvantageous because students can become well-rounded through many fields besides imaginative literature.

A public health student who studies history, for instance, may learn as much about human nature from the Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, as from any novel.
Studying that case teaches ethics, empathy and the dangers of power in a form directly relevant to her future work.
Such a case can build moral imagination just as effectively as a story, while also teaching real history.
Similarly, a literature student who takes a course in statistics gains a kind of breadth that poetry cannot give, yet few would argue that statistics should be required of everyone.

This shows that well-roundedness depends on breadth, not on any one [[canonical|canonical]] subject, so colleges should encourage an [[eclectic|eclectic]] mix of courses rather than literature in particular.
Second, compulsory literature courses can be disadvantageous when they turn reading into a chore.
Consider an engineering student forced to read long novels on a strict schedule while also preparing for difficult technical exams.
Rather than learning to love fiction, he may skim summaries, write [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] essays and leave college determined never to open a novel again.
Likewise, students in a required ethics course often memorize theories for the exam and forget them soon after, while those who choose the course tend to engage more deeply.
Requirements guarantee attendance, but they cannot guarantee interest or understanding.
This shows that imposing literature on unwilling students may [[alienate|alienate]] them from the very reading the requirement hopes to encourage.
A love of reading is more likely to grow from choice than from compulsion.
Admittedly, a requirement would be advantageous for students who would otherwise never encounter imaginative literature.
A student from a family without books, studying a technical subject, might discover in a mythology course a lifelong interest she would never have found on her own.
For her, the requirement would open a door that might otherwise stay closed for life.
Nevertheless, this benefit can be achieved by a broader humanities requirement in which literature is one option among history, philosophy and the arts.
A student like her could still choose the mythology course, while classmates with other interests could pursue history or philosophy instead.
This case therefore qualifies my position but does not reverse it, because breadth, not literature alone, is the real goal.
The goal of introducing new readers to great stories can be met without making one subject mandatory for all.
In conclusion, colleges should not require all students to read imaginative literature in order to become well-rounded.
Breadth can come from many fields, and forced reading can breed resentment, although exposure to the humanities helps students who would otherwise miss it.
A flexible humanities requirement, therefore, serves the goal of well-rounded graduates better than a single mandatory literature course.

essays.title: A funded semester abroad prepares global professionals

paragraphs.text: Some of the most important lessons in a person's education happen far from the lecture hall.
For this reason, many people argue that colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I largely agree with this recommendation, as long as universities provide financial support so that the requirement does not exclude poorer students.
A semester abroad prepares students for global problems, exposes them to different ways of working, and, despite real costs, can be made fair through careful planning.
First, requiring study abroad would be advantageous in fields where the most pressing problems cross national borders, because students need to see these problems from more than one country.
Consider the eradication of smallpox, which was declared in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign.
That campaign succeeded only because countries shared data and vaccine, and the people who led it had to work across languages, health systems and political interests.
A young doctor who has studied in another country is far better prepared for this kind of cooperation than one who has never left home.

Similarly, antibiotic resistance spreads easily across borders, so a pharmacy student in Vietnam who spends a semester in a country with strict prescription rules would return with practical ideas for reform.
This shows that, for disciplines facing global challenges, a required semester abroad is not a luxury but a sound investment in professional skill.
Second, a semester abroad would be valuable for students who might otherwise remain [[insular|insular]], because living in another culture challenges habits that seem natural at home.
In my own training as a physician in Vietnam, I assumed that the way my hospital organized ward rounds was the only reasonable way.
When I later observed colleagues in another country, I saw nurses speak openly to senior doctors, a practice that caught errors my own team might have missed.
That experience still shapes how I lead clinical teams today, more than any lecture I attended at home.
Likewise, a business student who studies in Japan may learn how long-term relationships with suppliers shape company decisions in ways that no textbook fully conveys.
Such experiences make graduates more [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] and more willing to question their own assumptions, which is exactly what a university education should achieve.
Admittedly, a mandatory semester abroad would not be advantageous in every circumstance, especially for students with limited money or heavy family duties.

A student from a poor rural family who works part-time to support younger siblings could not easily leave for four months, and an [[onerous|onerous]] requirement might push such a student to abandon college altogether.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for better design rather than for rejecting the recommendation.
Universities could offer scholarships, partner with institutions in nearby and less expensive countries, or allow short, intensive programs as an alternative for students in genuine hardship.

With these measures in place, the requirement would [[alleviate|alleviate]] rather than [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] inequality, since poorer students are often the ones who would never go abroad without institutional support.
A well-funded requirement would give them the same chance as their wealthier classmates.
In conclusion, I believe that universities should generally require a semester of study in a foreign country, provided they make it affordable for all.
Such a policy prepares students for problems that cross borders and broadens their habits of mind, and its main drawback, cost, can be reduced through planning.
The value of the requirement therefore depends less on the idea itself than on whether institutions are willing to fund it fairly.

essays.title: Encourage study abroad; do not require it

paragraphs.text: Travel is often praised as the best teacher, but not every valuable lesson needs to be compulsory.
Some argue that colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation: study abroad should be strongly encouraged and funded, but making it a requirement for all students would do more harm than good.

A universal requirement would burden students with fewer resources and disrupt programs with tight training sequences, and although study abroad is valuable, its benefits can be achieved through more flexible options.
First, a mandatory semester abroad would be disadvantageous in circumstances where students lack money or carry family duties, because the requirement would turn an opportunity into a barrier.
Consider a first-generation student in Vietnam whose parents are farmers and whose tuition is paid through loans.
For her, four months in Europe or the United States would mean extra costs for housing, flights and visas, as well as lost income from her part-time job.
Faced with this [[onerous|onerous]] condition, she might delay graduation or leave school entirely.
Similarly, a student who cares for an ill parent cannot simply move abroad for a semester, no matter how much he might benefit from the experience.
This shows that a universal rule, however well meant, would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] inequality, since it would fall hardest on the students whom universities most need to keep.
Second, the recommendation would be impractical in fields with tightly sequenced training, where a semester away can interrupt the development of essential skills.
In medical school, clinical rotations follow a strict order, and each one depends on supervised practice with local patients, local diseases and local laws.

A Vietnamese medical student who spent a semester abroad might learn interesting theory but would miss months of hands-on work with conditions such as dengue, which he will treat daily after graduation.
Likewise, engineering programs that require accredited laboratory courses may find that foreign credits do not transfer, forcing students to repeat work and delay their careers.
In such programs, the requirement would [[impede|impede]] rather than enrich professional preparation, and the cost would be paid later by the patients and clients these graduates serve.
Admittedly, studying abroad can be transformative, and the strongest case for the recommendation is that many students would never go unless they were required to.
A student who spends a semester in another country often returns more [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]], more confident and more aware that familiar practices are not the only reasonable ones.

Nevertheless, students who would not otherwise go abroad are usually held back by cost or family duties rather than by the lack of a rule, so these benefits can be extended to them without forcing every student to leave.

Universities could offer generous scholarships, short summer programs and joint online courses with foreign partners, and they could invite international students and visiting scholars to their own campuses.
These measures would bring the advantages of global exposure to many students while respecting those whose circumstances make a long stay abroad unwise.
A [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] policy of encouragement is therefore better than a blanket rule.
In conclusion, although study abroad has real value, colleges should not make it a requirement for graduation, at least not for every student in every program.
A mandatory semester would penalize poorer students and disrupt programs with strict training sequences, and its benefits can be achieved through more flexible means.
The best policy is to make study abroad possible for every student who wants it, rather than compulsory for those who cannot afford it.

worldly; familiar with and open to many cultures
practical and realistic rather than idealistic

essays.title: Reward teachers for student progress, carefully measured

paragraphs.text: In most professions, people who do excellent work expect to be rewarded for it.
This principle lies behind the recommendation that teachers' salaries should be based on the academic performance of their students.
I agree with this recommendation in a limited form: part of a teacher's pay should depend on students' academic progress, as long as progress is measured fairly and not by raw test scores alone.
Such a system would reward effective teaching, would direct attention to struggling students, and, despite the risk of gaming, can be designed to avoid its worst abuses.

First, linking some pay to student progress would be advantageous in school systems where pay depends only on years of service, because such systems give teachers little [[incentive|incentive]] to improve.
Consider a secondary school in which a dedicated young mathematics teacher spends her evenings redesigning lessons, and her students' scores rise steadily over two years.
Under a seniority scale, she earns less than a colleague who has taught from the same notes for twenty years and whose students make little progress.
Over time, she may leave teaching for a better-paid job in business.
Similarly, a district hospital that rewards its wards for lowering infection rates gives nurses a clear reason to follow hand-washing rules consistently.
This shows that when pay ignores results, the most capable teachers feel undervalued, and a modest link to student performance can help keep them in the classroom.
Second, performance-based pay would be beneficial where struggling students tend to be neglected, provided that the measure rewards improvement rather than final scores.
If a teacher's bonus depended on how much each student gained over the year, a child who began far behind would count as much as a top student.
A teacher in a poor rural district could then earn as much as one in a wealthy city school by helping weak readers catch up.
Likewise, a teacher with a class of recent immigrants would be rewarded for the students' rapid progress in a new language, even if their final scores remained modest.
Such a design makes the policy [[equitable|equitable]], because it measures what the teacher adds rather than what the student brought from home.
It also tells teachers that the children who need the most help are worth the most effort.
Admittedly, the strongest objection is that tying pay to test results can encourage teaching to the test or even dishonesty.
When scores alone determine rewards, some teachers may narrow their lessons to exam drills and neglect subjects such as art or history, and a few may be tempted to inflate grades.
Nevertheless, these risks argue for careful design rather than for abandoning the idea, just as the risk of side effects argues for careful dosing rather than for refusing all medicine.
A [[prudent|prudent]] system would use performance for only part of a salary, combine test gains with classroom observation and student feedback, and audit unusual jumps in scores.
With such safeguards, the [[pernicious|pernicious]] effects of purely test-based pay could be [[mitigated|mitigate]] while the benefits of rewarding good teaching are preserved.
In conclusion, I support basing a meaningful share of teachers' salaries on the academic progress of their students, but not on raw scores alone.
This approach would reward effective teachers, draw attention to students who are falling behind, and limit the risk of gaming through balanced measures.
Whether the policy helps or harms education depends on what it measures, so the measure must be designed as carefully as the reward.

essays.title: Test-based pay punishes teachers of poor students

paragraphs.text: What gets measured gets managed, but what gets measured is not always what matters most.
This warning applies directly to the recommendation that teachers' salaries should be based on the academic performance of their students.
I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because in most circumstances it would reward teachers for the advantages of their students rather than for the quality of their teaching.
Such a policy would penalize teachers in poor schools, would narrow what students learn, and, although it rightly values accountability, could be replaced by better ways of supporting good teaching.

First, performance-based pay would be disadvantageous in settings where students' results depend heavily on factors outside the classroom, because teachers would be judged on things they cannot control.

Consider two equally skilled teachers, one in a wealthy city school and one in a remote mountain district where many children are hungry, miss school during the harvest, and speak a minority language at home.
The first teacher's students will almost certainly score higher, so she would earn more even if her colleague worked twice as hard.
Over time, teachers would learn that the easiest way to raise their pay is to move to a richer school.
Similarly, in public health, judging a clinic only by its patients' outcomes would unfairly punish doctors who serve the sickest communities.
This shows that tying salaries to student performance would drive capable teachers away from the schools that need them most, an outcome that would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] existing inequality.
Second, the recommendation would be harmful wherever performance is measured by standardized tests, because teachers would reasonably focus on what is tested and neglect what is not.

Finland offers a useful contrast: it requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Its approach treats teachers as trusted professionals rather than as workers paid by output, and it gives them room to teach subjects that no exam can easily measure.
By contrast, a pay system based on scores would push many teachers toward [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] drills and away from projects, discussion and creative work.
Such narrowing would [[undermine|undermine]] the very purpose of education, which is to develop curious and independent thinkers, not merely good test takers.
Admittedly, the recommendation responds to a real problem: in systems where pay depends only on seniority, weak teachers face little pressure to improve.
A teacher who has delivered the same [[lackluster|lackluster]] lessons for years earns as much as an inspiring colleague, and students bear the cost.
Nevertheless, the solution to this problem is better evaluation and support, not salaries tied to student scores.

Schools could use regular classroom observation, peer mentoring and professional training, and they could reward teachers for taking on difficult assignments, guiding new colleagues or leading improvements in their departments.
These measures hold teachers accountable without blaming them for poverty or tempting them to teach only to the test, so the concern about accountability qualifies but does not reverse my position.
In conclusion, paying teachers according to their students' academic performance would, in most circumstances, do more harm than good.
It would punish teachers who serve disadvantaged children and narrow the curriculum, while the legitimate goal of accountability can be met through more [[equitable|equitable]] means.
If a society wants better teaching, it should invest in teachers, as Finland does, rather than turn their salaries into a gamble on test results.

essays.title: Shared heroes now mostly belong to history

paragraphs.text: Every age needs figures who show what human beings can achieve at their best.
Yet some argue that it is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero.
I largely agree with this claim, at least when "society" means a whole nation rather than a small community, because modern conditions make shared admiration of a living person extremely fragile.

Constant media exposure reveals every flaw, deeply divided societies rarely agree on anyone, and although some living people still earn wide respect, that respect seldom becomes lasting, shared hero status.
First, it has become very difficult to view a living person as a hero, because smartphones and social media expose every mistake to millions of people within hours.
In the past, a leader's private failings might remain hidden until long after death.
Today, an old post, a careless remark or a leaked recording can circulate worldwide in a single day, and smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
A respected scientist or athlete can therefore be [[lionized|lionize]] on Monday and [[disparaged|disparage]] on Friday.
Similarly, any public figure who speaks on a contested issue quickly attracts organized critics who search for past errors.
This shows that the constant scrutiny of modern media makes the spotless image of a hero almost impossible to sustain while the person is still alive.
Second, modern societies are often so [[polarized|polarized]] that no living figure can win the admiration of a whole population.

Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed mRNA research that allowed COVID-19 vaccines to be developed in under a year, and they won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
Yet their recognition did not end public suspicion of the vaccines their work made possible.
In many countries, debates over masks and lockdowns turned public health officials into heroes for some citizens and enemies for others.
Likewise, political leaders admired by one party are routinely portrayed as villains by the other, so even genuine achievements are judged through the lens of loyalty.
When admiration divides along group lines, a person may be a hero to a faction but not to the society, which is precisely what the claim describes.
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that ordinary people still perform heroic acts and are honored for them.
Doctors and nurses who worked long shifts during the pandemic were applauded in many countries, and firefighters who rescue children from burning buildings are still praised in local news.
Nevertheless, such recognition is usually [[ephemeral|ephemeral]] and local rather than lasting and shared by an entire society.
The applause for health workers faded within months, and few people remember the names of individual rescuers.
Full recognition often comes only after death, as with Ignaz Semmelweis, whose idea of hand washing most colleagues rejected in his lifetime and germ theory vindicated only years after he died.
These cases show that heroic acts still exist, but they do not [[negate|negate]] the claim, since brief local praise is not the lasting, shared admiration that makes someone a society's hero.
In conclusion, I largely agree that a modern society can no longer regard a living person as a hero in the full sense of the word.
Relentless media exposure and deep social divisions prevent lasting, shared admiration, even though individual acts of courage are still honored briefly.
Heroism has not disappeared, but its full recognition increasingly belongs to the dead, whose lives can finally be judged as a whole.

essays.title: Living heroes survive, though judged more realistically

paragraphs.text: It is fashionable to say that we live in a [[cynical|cynical]] age that no longer believes in heroes.
Following this view, some claim that it is no longer possible for a society to regard any living man or woman as a hero.

I mostly disagree with this claim: although modern scrutiny has made heroes harder to sustain, societies still recognize living people as heroes when their courage or service is clear and widely shared.

Living heroes still emerge in moments of crisis and in science and public service, and the strongest challenge to my view, the power of modern media to expose flaws, changes how heroes are seen but does not make them impossible.
First, societies continue to honor living people as heroes during crises, when the value of courage becomes obvious to everyone.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, doctors and nurses in Vietnam left their families for weeks to staff isolation hospitals, and many citizens wrote letters and sent food to thank them.
In my own field, I watched epidemiologists work through the night to trace contacts, and their communities thanked them openly.
Newspapers and neighbors described these health workers as heroes, and the word did not seem exaggerated.
Similarly, after natural disasters, rescuers who risk their lives to save strangers are widely praised as heroes while they are very much alive.
This shows that when a society faces a common threat, it readily treats the [[laudable|laudable]] sacrifices of its protectors as heroic, so the claim overstates the loss of public admiration.
Second, living scientists and public servants can earn heroic status when their work saves lives on a large scale.
Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed research on mRNA, and that work made it possible to develop COVID-19 vaccines in under a year.
When they won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, they were celebrated not merely as skilled researchers but as people whose persistence helped protect the world.
Their story is admired precisely because they continued their work when few people believed it mattered.

Likewise, a provincial health officer whose quick decisions stop a dengue outbreak may be publicly honored by the people she protected, which shows that careful judgment, not only dramatic courage, can still make someone a hero.
Such figures show that admiration for living people remains possible when their contribution is concrete and their motives seem [[disinterested|disinterested]].
Admittedly, the most compelling challenge to my position is that modern media make it easy to expose and exaggerate the flaws of any public figure.
Smartphones and social media spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow, so a respected person can be [[disparaged|disparage]] by thousands of strangers in a single day.
Even admired leaders now face constant criticism, and old mistakes can be revived at any moment.
Nevertheless, this scrutiny makes heroism more demanding, not impossible, because it tests whether admiration is deserved.
In fact, a hero who survives close examination may deserve more trust than the distant, idealized heroes of the past, whose failings were simply hidden.
Thus, the challenge [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: today's living heroes may be admired for specific acts rather than worshipped as perfect people, but they are still heroes.
In conclusion, I reject the claim that a society can no longer regard any living person as a hero.

Crises still produce widely admired figures, scientists and public servants still earn gratitude for lifesaving work, and media scrutiny, though intense, mainly forces societies to judge heroes more realistically.
What has changed is not our capacity for admiration but our demand that heroes be human rather than flawless.

essays.title: Collective success must sometimes come first

paragraphs.text: No society can satisfy every citizen at every moment.

This fact divides opinion: some people believe that in order to thrive, a society must put its own overall success before the well-being of its individual citizens, while others believe that a society's well-being can only be measured by the general welfare of all its people.
I lean toward the first view: a society must sometimes place collective goals above individual preferences, as long as those goals eventually serve the welfare of most citizens.

Collective priorities are necessary in public health and in economic development, and although the second view rightly warns against sacrificing vulnerable people, it offers little practical guidance for hard choices.
First, the first view is more realistic in public health, because protecting the population often requires limiting individual freedom.
When Vietnam passed its 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets, many riders complained that helmets were hot, inconvenient or expensive.
The government put the overall goal of road safety ahead of these personal preferences, and helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, reducing head injuries and deaths.
Similarly, the global WHO campaign that eradicated smallpox by 1980 depended on vaccination and data sharing that some individuals and governments found burdensome.
These cases show that a society which waits for every citizen's consent may fail to protect anyone, so placing collective success first is sometimes the only [[viable|viable]] path.
Second, economic development often requires short-term sacrifices by some citizens for the long-term strength of the nation.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, a change that disrupted many state enterprises and the workers who depended on them.
Many workers had to find new jobs, and some regions adjusted more slowly than others.
Yet a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Likewise, building a new highway or hospital may require relocating some families, even though the project benefits a whole province for decades.
Such policies put the nation's overall success first, but their [[salutary|salutary]] results eventually [[redounded|redound]] to the benefit of most citizens.
Admittedly, the second view captures an important truth: a society that ignores the welfare of its people risks becoming cruel.

The Tuskegee syphilis study, which withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent from 1932 to 1972, was carried out in the name of research, yet it inflicted [[grievous|grievous]] harm on its subjects.
Nevertheless, this example shows the danger of abusing collective goals, not the error of having them, since the study did not even serve the public good it claimed to serve.
The outrage that followed led to US rules requiring ethics review boards, which allow research to serve society while protecting individuals.

Thus, the second view is best understood as a necessary limit on the first rather than a replacement for it: a society should pursue collective success, but never by [[flouting|flout]] the basic rights of its citizens.
In conclusion, I side more closely with the view that a thriving society must sometimes put its overall success ahead of individual well-being.

Public health laws and economic reforms show that collective priorities can benefit nearly everyone in the end, while the history of research abuses shows why such priorities need firm ethical limits.
The real test of a society, then, is not whether it ever asks individuals to sacrifice, but whether those sacrifices serve the common good.

essays.title: A society thrives only if its people do

paragraphs.text: A country can grow richer every year while many of its people grow poorer.

This possibility lies at the heart of a debate: some people believe that a society must put its own overall success before the well-being of its individual citizens, whereas others believe that a society's well-being can only be measured by the general welfare of all its people.
I side with the second view, because success that leaves large groups behind is neither real nor lasting, although I accept that individuals must sometimes make temporary sacrifices.

Policies that ignore individuals tend to cause lasting harm, true national strength is built on the welfare of ordinary people, and the first view's valid point about collective effort fits within the second view rather than against it.
First, the second view is closer to the truth because a society that sacrifices individuals in the name of progress often damages itself.
In the Tuskegee syphilis study, which ran from 1932 to 1972, researchers withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent.
The result was [[grievous|grievous]] harm to the men and their families, followed by public outrage that led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.
Similarly, a city that clears a poor neighborhood for a new highway without fair compensation may gain a faster road, but it leaves many families poorer and distrustful of their government.
These cases show that when a society treats its citizens as means to an end, its supposed success proves hollow, and it must later [[redress|redress]] the damage.
Second, lasting national success is itself built on the well-being of ordinary people, so measuring a society by general welfare is the most accurate test.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Families who own their homes can plan for the future, invest in their children's education and face economic shocks with more security.
This policy treats a decent home as part of national success rather than as a reward for it.
Likewise, Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms are rightly judged a success not only because rice exports grew, but because poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Such examples show that the most useful measure of a society's health is how its people live, which is exactly what the second view proposes.
Admittedly, the first view is right that a society sometimes needs individuals to accept limits for the common good.
Vietnam's 2007 helmet law forced riders to accept discomfort, yet it raised helmet use to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.
Nevertheless, this law succeeded precisely because it protected individual citizens, not because it placed an abstract national goal above them.
Riders accepted a small cost in comfort in exchange for a large gain in personal safety.
Its value was measured in lives saved and injuries prevented, which is the language of general welfare rather than national prestige.

Thus, the first view's strongest example actually supports the second: a [[prudent|prudent]] society may ask for sacrifices, but only when those sacrifices [[ameliorate|ameliorate]] the lives of its people.
In conclusion, I agree more with the view that a society's well-being is measured by the welfare of all its people.

Policies that sacrifice individuals tend to fail both morally and practically, real national strength rests on ordinary citizens' security, and even justified collective demands earn their legitimacy by benefiting individuals.
A nation that pursues [[equitable|equitable]] welfare will find that its overall success follows from, rather than competes with, the well-being of its citizens.

essays.title: Treat facts as provisional, not as permanent

paragraphs.text: The history of knowledge is full of certainties that later collapsed.

Drawing on this history, some claim that any piece of information referred to as a fact should be mistrusted, because much of the information that people assume is factual later turns out to be inaccurate.

I partly agree with both the claim and the reason: we should treat facts as provisional and remain open to revising them, although "mistrust" should mean careful questioning rather than outright rejection.

The claim is sound when applied to new or single findings, the reason is well supported by history, and the strongest objection, that constant doubt would make action impossible, can be answered by separating doubt from paralysis.
First, the claim is largely justified when it comes to new findings, because a single result labeled as a fact may not survive further testing.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Many of these findings had been cited in textbooks and news articles as facts about human behavior.
Similarly, in my own work as an epidemiologist, I have seen early studies suggest that a drug or exposure has a strong effect, only for larger studies to show a much weaker one.
This shows that a [[credulous|credulous]] acceptance of anything called a fact is risky, and that the claim's call for mistrust is reasonable when evidence is thin or comes from a single study.
Second, the reason on which the claim is based is supported by history, since much information once assumed to be factual did turn out to be false.
For centuries, it was considered a fact that the sun moved around the Earth, and in 1633 the Church forced Galileo to recant his support for the opposite view.
Today his position is accepted by everyone, and the earlier "fact" is remembered only as an error that authority once defended.
Likewise, around 1960, thalidomide was given to pregnant women as a sedative on the assumption that it was safe, yet it caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe.
These cases confirm the reason: confident labels do not guarantee accuracy, so a degree of doubt toward any fact is not [[cynical|cynical]] but [[prudent|prudent]].
Admittedly, the most serious objection is that mistrusting every fact would make decisions impossible, since people must act on the best information they have.
A doctor who refused to trust established facts about hand washing or vaccines would endanger patients rather than protect them.
Nevertheless, the claim can be read in a moderate way: to mistrust a fact is to keep checking it, not to ignore it.

Ignaz Semmelweis showed this attitude in Vienna in 1847: instead of accepting the beliefs of his time about childbed fever, he had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths on his ward fell sharply.
In this sense, mistrust is a [[judicious|judicious]] habit of verification, and the objection [[qualifies|qualify]] my agreement rather than reverses it.
In conclusion, I partly agree that facts deserve some mistrust, because the reason given, that many accepted facts prove inaccurate, is well supported.
Failed replications and historical errors show the value of doubt, while the need to act on the best available knowledge shows that doubt must remain measured.
The wisest response to a fact is neither blind faith nor automatic rejection, but continued testing in light of new evidence.
