essays.title: Well-tested facts deserve our trust

paragraphs.text: Knowledge advances by correcting its mistakes, but that does not make all knowledge unreliable.

Some claim that any piece of information referred to as a fact should be mistrusted, since it may be proven false in the future, and they base this claim on the reason that much of the information people assume is factual turns out to be inaccurate.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason: although some facts are revised, well-tested facts deserve trust, and occasional errors do not justify general mistrust.

The claim would make practical life impossible, the reason exaggerates how often established facts fail, and while skepticism toward new findings is wise, it does not support distrusting facts as a whole.
First, the claim is unworkable, because people and institutions must act on established facts every day.
In 1847, Ignaz Semmelweis had doctors in Vienna wash their hands in chlorinated lime, and deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply.
Yet most of his colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.
Their doubt looked like caution, but it delayed a simple practice that could have saved many patients.
Similarly, a parent who mistrusted the fact that vaccines prevent disease might refuse protection for her children, putting them and others at risk.

These cases show that a general policy of mistrust, which the claim recommends, would [[impede|impede]] the very progress it seeks to protect, since every useful discovery must at some point be trusted enough to be used.
Second, the reason itself is [[dubious|dubious]], because the facts that turn out to be wrong are usually early or poorly tested, not those confirmed by many independent sources.
It is true that in 2015 a large collaboration could reproduce the results of only about a third of 100 published psychology studies.
But this failure involved single, new findings, and the replication effort was itself the scientific method correcting them.
In other words, the study shows that science detects its own errors, not that every fact deserves suspicion.
By contrast, the fact that smallpox vaccination works has been confirmed so thoroughly that it is effectively [[incontrovertible|incontrovertible]]; indeed, smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980.
Thus, the reason confuses the fragile early stage of knowledge with its well-established core, and it cannot support mistrust of all facts.
Admittedly, a degree of doubt toward claims called facts is healthy, especially when they come from a single study or from sources with a stake in the result.
Thalidomide, given to pregnant women as a sedative around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, and Frances Kelsey of the US FDA was right to refuse approval.
Nevertheless, Kelsey's caution was a call for better evidence, not a rejection of facts as such.
The US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962, which strengthened the process for establishing facts rather than abandoning it.
In other words, the lesson of such errors is to match our confidence to the strength of the [[empirical|empirical]] evidence, which is very different from the blanket mistrust the claim recommends.
In conclusion, I reject the claim that anything called a fact should be mistrusted, and I find its supporting reason exaggerated.

Blanket mistrust would make action impossible, most revised facts were weakly established in the first place, and healthy skepticism is best expressed by improving evidence rather than doubting everything.
Facts are not [[infallible|infallible]], but well-tested ones remain the best guide we have.

essays.title: In severe crises, basic needs come first

paragraphs.text: When a family's income collapses, it buys rice before it buys concert tickets.

Some argue that nations should behave in the same way, claiming that governments should suspend funding for the arts when significant numbers of citizens are hungry or unemployed, since it is inappropriate, and perhaps cruel, to use public resources for art while basic needs go unmet.

I partly agree with both the claim and the reason: during a genuine crisis, governments should temporarily redirect arts funding toward food and jobs, although a complete suspension should be a last resort.
The claim is sound when resources are truly scarce, the reason rightly appeals to the priority of survival, and although art has real value in hard times, that value does not outweigh hunger.
First, the claim is justified in situations where public money is severely limited, because every budget decision then has a direct human cost.
Consider a poor province after a flood destroys its harvest, leaving thousands of families without food or income.
If its government spends funds on a new theater festival rather than on emergency rations and public works jobs, it chooses a [[trifling|trifling]] pleasure over survival.
Each meal it fails to provide is a cost borne by a child, not by an abstract line in a budget.
Similarly, in Vietnam before the Doi Moi reforms of 1986, when the country faced food shortages, feeding the population was rightly the government's first duty.
This shows that in moments of real scarcity, suspending arts funding is not hostility toward culture but a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] ordering of priorities.
Second, the reason behind the claim is largely persuasive, since public resources come from all citizens and should first serve their most [[pressing|pressing]] needs.
In medicine, we follow a similar principle: a district hospital that lacks antibiotics and oxygen does not spend its limited budget on sculptures for its lobby.
As a physician, I would find it hard to justify such spending to the families waiting in the corridor for treatment.
Likewise, unemployed workers who see public money supporting an expensive opera season may reasonably feel [[alienated|alienate]] from a government that seems indifferent to their struggles.
Thus, the reason is right that using public funds for the arts during widespread hunger can appear cruel, and such appearances [[undermine|undermine]] public trust.
Admittedly, the strongest point on the other side is that arts funding is small and that art can help people endure hard times.
During economic crises, public art projects can employ jobless painters, musicians and builders, and community performances can offer comfort to struggling families.
Nevertheless, these benefits support redirecting arts funding toward projects that create jobs or serve the poor, not continuing business as usual.
A government could, for instance, pause grants to elite institutions while paying local artists to teach children or decorate public spaces built by unemployed workers.

This compromise [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: the claim is right about priorities, but "suspend" should mean temporarily reshaping arts spending rather than abolishing it, and normal funding should return once the crisis eases.
In conclusion, I partly agree that nations should suspend ordinary arts funding when many citizens are hungry or jobless.
Severe scarcity makes basic needs the clear priority, the reason correctly warns that ignoring those needs can be cruel, and the value of art is best preserved by linking it to relief.
The test of such a policy is whether it puts people first in a crisis without permanently abandoning the culture that gives their lives meaning.

essays.title: Cutting arts funding feeds no one

paragraphs.text: In hard times, it is tempting to treat art as a luxury.

Some therefore claim that nations should suspend government funding for the arts whenever significant numbers of citizens are hungry or unemployed, reasoning that it is inappropriate, even cruel, to spend public money on the arts while basic needs remain unmet.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason: cutting arts funding would do little to relieve hunger, while it would harm workers, communities and a nation's long-term future.
The claim rests on a false trade-off, the reason misunderstands what the arts provide in hard times, and although basic needs must come first, protecting them does not require abandoning art.
First, the claim is flawed because arts funding is usually a small part of public budgets, so suspending it would not meaningfully reduce hunger or unemployment.
Consider a country with a large health and welfare budget and a modest arts grant program.

Canceling the arts grants might pay for a few days of food aid, but it would also close theaters and museums that employ actors, technicians, guards and cleaners, adding to the very unemployment the policy claims to address.
The money saved would be small, but the jobs lost would be real.
Similarly, a craft village whose workshops attract visitors would lose income if public support for local festivals disappeared.
This shows that the claim's choice between bread and art is largely [[specious|specious]], since art itself provides livelihoods.
Second, the reason is unconvincing because it treats art as a luxury for the comfortable, when artists themselves are often poor and their work often helps struggling communities most.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime, yet he is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
His career reminds us that artists often work without market rewards and need support precisely when markets ignore them.
Likewise, during dengue control campaigns in Vietnam, I have seen simple songs, posters and street performances explain prevention to villagers far more effectively than official leaflets.
Health workers and local artists worked together, and families remembered the messages long after the campaign ended.
Thus, public art is not a cruel indulgence but a tool that can [[edify|edify]] and unite people in difficult times, which [[undermines|undermine]] the reason behind the claim.
Admittedly, the reason contains an important moral truth: a government that funds lavish spectacles while children go hungry has lost its sense of priority.
If a ministry spent heavily on a grand new opera house during a famine, citizens would be right to feel betrayed.
Nevertheless, this concern justifies careful choices within arts spending, not a complete suspension that would punish modest community programs along with extravagant ones.
Governments can favor modest community programs over prestige projects and link arts grants to employment, while funding food and job programs through larger parts of the budget.
In this way, the legitimate worry about cruelty can be addressed without [[jettisoning|jettison]] a public good whose value lasts far longer than any crisis and often helps a society recover from it.
In conclusion, I largely reject the claim that arts funding should be suspended whenever many citizens are hungry or unemployed, and I find its reason only partly convincing.
Cutting such funding would barely help the poor, the arts often serve struggling communities directly, and the real danger of misplaced priorities can be met through wiser spending.
A nation recovering from hardship needs both bread and meaning, and it should not sacrifice one for a [[nominal|nominal]] gain in the other.

essays.title: Laws alone cannot change hearts

paragraphs.text: Societies often respond to every new problem by passing a new law.
Yet some claim that many problems of modern society cannot be solved by laws and the legal system, because laws cannot change what is in people's hearts or minds.
I largely agree with both the claim and the reason, although I believe laws can play a supporting role when they are combined with education and changes in social norms.

Many modern problems depend on private choices that laws cannot easily reach, laws that ignore beliefs are often evaded, and while some laws do change behavior quickly, lasting change still depends on persuasion.
First, the claim is largely true because many modern problems arise from countless private choices that the legal system cannot monitor.
Antibiotic resistance, a problem I study as an epidemiologist, is a clear case.

Even where rules restrict antibiotic sales, overuse and over-the-counter sales remain common in many countries, including Vietnam, helping resistant bacteria spread so that drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
In my own work, I have met pharmacists who know the risks but sell antibiotics anyway because customers demand them and competitors will not refuse.
Similarly, loneliness and online misinformation are problems that no court can [[redress|redress]] through rulings alone.

This shows that when a problem lives in [[ingrained|ingrained]] habits and private beliefs, the legal system can at best [[mitigate|mitigate]] it, while real solutions must come from education and trust.
Second, the reason is persuasive, because laws that conflict with people's beliefs are often evaded or resented.
In 1633, the Church forced Galileo to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
The ruling silenced him publicly but did not change the evidence or the minds of those who studied it, and his view eventually prevailed.
Authorities could punish dissent and ban books, but they could not force belief.
Likewise, Ignaz Semmelweis showed in 1847 that hand washing reduced deaths from childbed fever, yet no order could have made his doubtful colleagues accept an idea they rejected.

These cases show that coercion can change outward behavior but rarely inner conviction, which is precisely what the reason asserts; a law that people regard as unjust may even harden their resistance.
Admittedly, the most compelling counterexample is that some laws change behavior quickly and eventually change attitudes too.
Vietnam's 2007 helmet law raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths, and today wearing a helmet is simply normal.
Nevertheless, this success depended on conditions that many problems lack: the required behavior was simple, visible and easy to enforce at the roadside.
Problems such as prejudice, poor diet or the misuse of medicines involve hidden, repeated choices that no police officer can observe and that people may defend as personal freedom.
Thus, the helmet law [[qualifies|qualify]] the claim rather than refutes it: laws can solve narrow, visible problems, but many modern problems require persuasion that the legal system cannot supply.
In conclusion, I largely agree that laws alone cannot solve many of modern society's problems, and that their limits lie in their inability to change hearts and minds.
Private choices escape legal control, imposed rules often meet quiet resistance, and even successful laws work best when behavior is simple to enforce.
Laws are therefore most effective as one tool among many, supported by education, personal example and [[ardent|ardent]] public persuasion that reaches people where laws cannot.

essays.title: Laws can reshape both behavior and beliefs

paragraphs.text: It is often said that you cannot legislate morality, and that only education can make people better.
In the same spirit, some claim that many problems of modern society cannot be solved by laws and the legal system, because laws cannot change what is in people's hearts or minds.
I mostly disagree with both the claim and the reason: although laws are not sufficient by themselves, they have solved many social problems and can, over time, change attitudes as well as actions.

Laws have solved serious modern problems, they often change beliefs by changing habits, and while some problems do resist legal solutions, this shows the need for better laws rather than the futility of law.
First, the claim underestimates what laws can accomplish, because many serious problems have been reduced mainly through legal action.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets is a striking example.
Before the law, many riders resisted helmets as hot or unnecessary, yet helmet use rose from low levels to over 90% within months, and head injuries and deaths fell.
In my own clinical work, I have seen far fewer young riders with severe head injuries than senior colleagues describe from earlier years.
Similarly, after the Tuskegee syphilis study withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent, US rules requiring ethics review boards changed how research on people is conducted.
These cases show that a well-designed law can solve problems far faster than voluntary change alone, especially when the required behavior is clear.
Second, the reason is mistaken, because laws can change hearts and minds indirectly by changing what people regularly do and see.

The Montgomery bus boycott of 1955-1956 helped end bus segregation in that city, and once Black and white residents shared buses as equals, an arrangement that had seemed unthinkable began to seem ordinary.
Changing the rules changed daily experience, and daily experience slowly changed attitudes in ways that speeches alone had not.
Likewise, in cities that banned smoking in restaurants, many diners who once [[balked|balk]] at the rule now regard smoke-free dining as normal.
This shows that the law is not only a [[deterrent|deterrent]] but also a teacher: by making a behavior normal, it gradually reshapes the beliefs behind it.
Admittedly, some modern problems do resist legal solutions, especially those rooted in private choices that are hard to observe.
Antibiotic overuse and over-the-counter sales remain common in many countries, including Vietnam, and resistant bacteria continue to spread even where rules exist.
Nevertheless, this failure reflects weak enforcement and poor design, not a basic limit of law, since rules that are rarely enforced teach people that they can be ignored.

Stronger pharmacy inspections, electronic prescription records and penalties for illegal sales could make antibiotic rules as [[efficacious|efficacious]] as helmet rules, especially if combined with public education.
Thus, the problems that laws have not yet solved show the need for smarter legal tools, not that law itself is [[futile|futile]], and the helmet law shows what good design can achieve.
In conclusion, I reject the claim that the legal system cannot solve many modern problems, as well as the reason that laws cannot reach hearts and minds.
Laws have reduced deaths and abuses, they reshape beliefs by reshaping habits, and their failures usually point to poor design rather than [[inherent|inherent]] weakness.
Laws work best alongside education, but dismissing them would leave society without one of its most powerful tools for change.

essays.title: Student interests make learning stick

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has sat through a dull lecture knows that attention is the first condition of learning.
For this reason, some recommend that educators should take students' interests into account when planning the content of the courses they teach.
I largely agree with this recommendation, provided that students' interests shape how core content is selected and framed rather than replace that core content.

Considering interests would be advantageous for motivating students and for connecting lessons to real problems, and, despite the risk of a shallow curriculum, it can be balanced with essential knowledge.
First, taking students' interests into account would be advantageous in courses where students lack motivation, because interest turns passive listeners into active learners.
Consider a statistics course for medical students who see the subject as an [[arcane|arcane]] hurdle.

When I teach such students, I build lessons around data from dengue outbreaks or hospital infections, problems they already care about, and they ask far more questions than when the same methods are taught with abstract examples.
Similarly, a history teacher who lets students choose a local topic for their projects often finds that even quiet students become [[avid|avid]] researchers.
This shows that interest is not a distraction from learning but a [[catalyst|catalyst]] for it, which is why educators should consider it when planning content.
Motivated students also study more on their own, which multiplies the effect of every hour spent in class.
Second, the recommendation would be advantageous in circumstances where course content risks becoming detached from the problems students will face.

A public health course in Vietnam, for instance, could include a unit on antibiotic resistance, since overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics help resistant bacteria spread and students see the consequences in their own families.

Alexander Fleming warned in his 1945 Nobel lecture that misuse would breed resistant bacteria, a warning students find far more striking when they have watched a relative buy antibiotics without a prescription.
Likewise, a computer science course that includes projects on ride-hailing or delivery apps, which grew out of GPS technology, connects theory to tools students use every day.
When content reflects students' real concerns, it becomes more [[germane|germane]] and more memorable, and students are more likely to apply it after the course ends.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which following students' interests would not be advantageous, particularly when those interests are narrow or uninformed.
Students in a basic chemistry course might prefer to study only dramatic topics such as explosions, while skipping the careful work on measurement and safety that every later course requires.
Others might ask to drop difficult but essential subjects altogether, such as the mathematics behind chemical reactions.
Nevertheless, this risk calls for balance rather than rejection of the recommendation.

A teacher can keep the essential topics fixed while using students' interests to choose examples, projects and readings; the chemistry teacher, for example, could teach measurement and safety through experiments with cooking or cleaning products.
In this way, interests guide the path through the material without lowering the destination, so the concern [[qualifies|qualify]] rather than reverses my position.
In conclusion, educators should generally take students' interests into account when designing course content, as long as core knowledge remains protected.
Doing so motivates learners and connects lessons to real problems, while the danger of a shallow curriculum can be managed through careful design.
The best courses meet students where they are and then lead them, step by step, further than they expected to go.

essays.title: Expertise, not preference, should set course content

paragraphs.text: Students are the best judges of what bores them, but not always of what they need.
This distinction matters for the recommendation that educators should take students' interests into account when planning the content of the courses they teach.

I mostly disagree with this recommendation as it applies to course content: students' interests should shape teaching methods, but what a course covers should be decided mainly by educators' expertise and the needs of the field.

Students often cannot know what they will need, following interests can leave dangerous gaps, and although interest improves motivation, that benefit can be achieved without letting it determine content.

First, adopting the recommendation would be disadvantageous in fields where students cannot yet judge which knowledge will matter, because their interests reflect present tastes rather than future needs.
For decades, research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman was little-noticed, and few students would have chosen to study it.
Yet that basic research made it possible to develop COVID-19 vaccines in under a year, and it earned the two scientists the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Similarly, many medical students find biochemistry dull, yet it is the basis for understanding how drugs work and why they fail, and a doctor who skipped it would struggle to explain treatment to patients.
This shows that interest is a poor guide to what will prove [[germane|germane]] to a career, and that educators, who see the whole field and its history, are better placed to decide content.
Second, the recommendation would be harmful in professional programs such as medicine and engineering, where gaps in content can endanger other people.

A pharmacology course that skipped antibiotic resistance because students preferred newer topics would produce doctors and pharmacists unprepared for a real threat: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
As an epidemiologist, I have seen young clinicians prescribe antibiotics for viral fevers, a habit that better training could have prevented.
Likewise, an engineering course that let students skip safety codes in favor of exciting design projects would put future buildings and their occupants at risk.
In such fields, a curriculum shaped by preference rather than necessity would be [[myopic|myopic]], and its costs would fall on patients and the public rather than on the students themselves.
Admittedly, students learn more when they are interested, and ignoring their interests entirely would make teaching [[lackluster|lackluster]] and ineffective.
A teacher who presents statistics through dengue outbreak data, for example, will hold the attention of medical students far better than one who relies on abstract formulas alone.
Nevertheless, this benefit concerns how content is taught, not what content is chosen.

Finland, which requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree and treats teaching as a respected and selective profession, shows the value of trusting trained educators to make such professional judgments.

Thus, interests should [[inform|inform]] examples, projects and teaching style, while the core content remains the responsibility of [[erudite|erudite]] teachers who understand what students will need years later.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that students' interests should determine the content of courses, though they should influence how that content is taught.
Students cannot always foresee what knowledge they will need, gaps in essential content can harm the public, and the motivational value of interest can be captured through teaching methods.
The teacher's task is to make necessary knowledge interesting, not to make interesting knowledge the only knowledge taught.

essays.title: Technology should buy back people's time

paragraphs.text: Nearly every major invention, from the washing machine to the smartphone, has promised to give people back some of their time.
Whether that promise should be the central purpose of technology, however, is a question worth examining.

I largely agree that the primary goal of technological advancement should be to increase people's efficiency so that they have more leisure time, as long as the time saved is protected rather than simply filled with more work.
Efficiency frees people from draining routine labor, leisure supports health and creativity, and, admittedly, a few fields such as medicine must put other goals first.
First, efficiency is a worthy primary goal because much of human labor is repetitive and exhausting, and technology that removes it improves lives directly.
Consider a district hospital in rural Vietnam where nurses once spent hours copying patient records by hand at the end of every shift.
When the hospital adopted a simple electronic record system, the same tasks took minutes, and nurses could go home on time instead of staying late.
They felt less tired, and many spent the recovered evenings with their families.
Similarly, the washing machine turned a full day of laundry into a task that runs in the background, giving households hours back every week.
These cases show that when technology targets [[onerous|onerous]] routine work, the efficiency it creates turns directly into leisure, exactly as the statement envisions.
The statement is therefore most convincing when it describes technologies designed for everyday tasks at work and at home.
Second, the leisure that efficiency creates is not wasted time; it is the space in which people rest, learn and create.
In my own work as an epidemiologist, statistical software now runs in seconds an analysis that once took days of manual calculation.
I do not spend the saved hours idly; I use them to read, to rest and to think about better research questions, which ultimately makes my work more useful.
Likewise, a doctor who has had enough rest is far less likely to make a dangerous mistake than one who has worked without a break.
This suggests that leisure is not a luxury but a resource, so technology that expands it can [[alleviate|alleviate]] fatigue and improve the quality of the work that remains.
Rest, in other words, is part of what makes people productive, not merely a reward for being so.
Admittedly, efficiency and leisure cannot be the primary goal of every technology.
The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines, developed in under a year thanks to decades of basic research by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, were designed to save lives, not to save time.
Nevertheless, such exceptions are few, and even technologies built for other purposes often deliver their widest benefits by saving people time.
GPS, for instance, was built by the US military for its own purposes, yet once it was opened to civilians it became the basis of navigation and delivery apps that save people countless hours.
This consideration [[qualifies|qualify]] my position: efficiency should be the main goal of everyday consumer technology, while fields such as medicine may legitimately put safety and survival first.
In conclusion, I largely agree that technology should mainly aim to make people more efficient so that they enjoy more leisure, provided that the time saved actually reaches them.
Efficiency removes draining work, leisure fuels health and creativity, and only a few fields, such as medicine, require different priorities.
If employers and governments ensure that saved hours become free hours rather than extra tasks, technological progress will fulfill its most [[salutary|salutary]] promise.

essays.title: Technology should solve problems, not just save time

paragraphs.text: We live surrounded by machines that save time, yet many people feel busier than ever.
This paradox raises the question of what technological advancement should mainly try to achieve.

I mostly disagree that the primary goal of technological advancement should be to increase efficiency for the sake of leisure; its primary goal should be to [[ameliorate|ameliorate]] serious human problems, although efficiency often helps it do so.
The greatest technologies have protected life rather than saved time, efficiency gains rarely become leisure by themselves, and, admittedly, efficiency still matters in everyday life.
First, the most valuable technologies in history have aimed at survival and health, not at free time.
Smallpox, for example, was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.
The aim of that effort was not to make anyone more efficient; it was to end a disease that had killed and disfigured people for centuries.
Similarly, releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia.
These cases show that if technology were judged mainly by the leisure it creates, its most [[profound|profound]] achievements would rank below a faster dishwasher, which is plainly absurd.
Health, safety and survival must come first, and leisure is meaningful only for people who are alive and well enough to enjoy it.
Second, efficiency gains seldom turn into leisure on their own, so making leisure the primary goal sets technology up to fail by its own standard.
In Vietnamese hospitals where I have worked, messaging apps were supposed to save doctors time, yet they mainly allowed supervisors to send requests late at night.
The work became faster, but the working day became longer and less clearly [[circumscribed|circumscribe]].
Doctors answered messages over dinner, and several colleagues told me they felt more exhausted than before the apps arrived.
Likewise, smartphones let people answer emails anywhere, which often means that they answer emails everywhere, even on holiday.
This shows that whether saved time becomes leisure depends on employers, laws and habits rather than on the technology itself, so leisure is a poor yardstick for deciding what to build.
The statement, in short, assumes a link between efficiency and free time that real workplaces often break.
Admittedly, efficiency is valuable, and some technologies do give people real free time.
GPS, first built by the US military, now guides drivers and delivery riders through unfamiliar cities, sparing them hours of getting lost.
Nevertheless, GPS matters mainly because it made travel safer and new services possible, not because it lengthened anyone's weekend.
In the same way, the washing machine saved hours of labor, but its deeper value lay in freeing people for education and paid work.
Efficiency, then, is best seen as a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] means that helps technology meet human needs, not as the end that should define its purpose.
The statement therefore holds only in a narrow sense, while its broader claim about technology's primary goal does not.
In conclusion, I disagree that efficiency for the sake of leisure should be the primary goal of technology, although I accept that efficiency is often a useful tool.
The greatest technologies have saved lives, efficiency rarely becomes free time by itself, and even time-saving tools matter most for the broader needs they serve.
Inventors and funders should therefore ask first which problem a technology solves, and only then how much time it saves.

essays.title: Assess understanding, not memorized facts

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has crammed for an exam knows how quickly memorized facts fade once the test is over.
This common experience lies behind the recommendation that educators should assess students' ability to explain ideas, trends and concepts rather than their grasp of facts.
I largely agree with this recommendation, particularly in advanced and professional education, as long as students first learn the basic facts that explanation requires.
Explanation-based assessment rewards lasting understanding, it prepares students for real work, and, admittedly, it may be premature for beginners who still lack essential facts.
First, in a setting where the goal is long-term understanding, adopting the recommendation would be advantageous because explaining an idea requires a deeper grasp than recalling it.
Consider a medical school course on infectious diseases.

A student who has memorized that antibiotics are sold over the counter in many countries, including Vietnam, knows a fact, but a student who can explain how overuse helps resistant bacteria spread understands why drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Only the second student can apply that knowledge to a new drug or a new country.
Similarly, Finland relies far less on standardized testing than many countries and trusts its highly trained teachers to judge how well students understand ideas.
These cases suggest that assessing explanation pushes students beyond [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] memorization toward the kind of understanding the recommendation values.
In such settings, a test that asks students to explain is simply a better test.
Second, in professional training, judging students by their explanations is advantageous because real work rarely asks for isolated facts.

In my work as an epidemiologist, no one asks me to recite the number of dengue cases in a single year; health officials ask me to explain why cases rise in certain seasons and which interventions might help.
Explaining such trends requires me to connect rainfall, mosquito breeding and human movement, not to repeat isolated numbers.
A trainee who can interpret such trends is far more useful to a health department than one who has merely memorized tables.

Likewise, a business student who can explain why Kodak, whose own engineer invented the digital camera, was slow to embrace digital photography has learned a lesson that will [[inform|inform]] future decisions.
This shows that explanation-based assessment measures the skill graduates actually need, which is the recommendation's central strength.
Employers and patients, after all, depend on graduates who can reason with knowledge, not merely store it.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which adopting the recommendation would not be advantageous, especially for beginners.

A first-year pharmacology student who cannot remember basic drug doses cannot safely explain treatment strategies, and a child who does not know the order of major events cannot meaningfully discuss historical trends.
Nevertheless, this objection shows that facts are a foundation, not that they should be the final target of assessment.
A sensible program can test core facts briefly in the early years and then shift most of its assessment toward explanation as students advance.
This circumstance therefore [[qualifies|qualify]] my position rather than overturning it: facts deserve some assessment, but explanation should carry the greater weight.
In conclusion, I largely agree that educators should assess students mainly on their ability to explain the ideas, trends and concepts behind the facts.
Such assessment rewards lasting understanding and prepares students for real work, although beginners still need a solid base of [[germane|germane]] facts.
The best approach treats facts as the starting point and explanation as the goal, shifting the balance as students mature.

essays.title: Facts must stay central to assessment

paragraphs.text: A brilliant explanation built on a wrong fact is still wrong.
This simple point matters for the recommendation that educators should assess students' ability to explain ideas, trends and concepts instead of their grasp of facts.

Although explanation is important, I mostly disagree with this recommendation, because in many settings a firm grasp of facts is what makes sound explanation possible and must therefore be assessed directly.
Facts protect safety in high-stakes fields, fact-based assessment is fairer and more precise, and, admittedly, explanation deserves more weight in advanced study.
First, in fields where errors carry serious consequences, assessing facts is essential because explanation without accurate knowledge can be dangerous.
Consider a nursing student who can explain the general principles of drug safety but cannot recall the correct dose of a common medicine.
On a hospital ward, that student could harm a patient despite understanding the theory well.

The thalidomide disaster, in which a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960 caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe, shows how much depends on precise knowledge of a drug's effects.
Similarly, pilots are tested on exact emergency procedures, not merely on the concepts of flight.
In such circumstances, adopting the recommendation would be [[deleterious|deleterious]], because it would allow students to pass while lacking knowledge on which other people's safety depends.
Here, facts are not a lower form of learning; they are the minimum standard of competence.
Second, assessing facts is advantageous because it is more objective and therefore fairer to students from different backgrounds.
In Vietnam, many rural students have had less exposure to discussion-based teaching than their urban peers, and some are shy about speaking at length.
If assessment rewarded fluent explanation above all, these students might be judged by their speaking style rather than by what they actually know.
By contrast, a question about a fact has a clear right answer, so two teachers grading it will usually agree.
Grades for open explanations, however, often depend on each teacher's taste and can vary widely.
This shows that fact-based assessment offers a fairness and precision that explanation-based grading often lacks, which [[undermines|undermine]] the recommendation's call to stop assessing facts.
A recommendation that ignores this advantage risks rewarding confidence rather than knowledge.
Admittedly, there are circumstances in which focusing on explanation would be advantageous, especially in advanced study and research training.

In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, which shows that young researchers must learn to question and explain findings rather than simply accept them.
Nevertheless, even this skill depends on facts, because a student cannot judge whether a result is [[plausible|plausible]] without knowing what earlier studies found.
An epidemiology trainee who does not know the basic facts of how dengue spreads, for example, cannot judge whether a surprising new study deserves trust.
This consideration narrows my position rather than reversing it: explanation should be added to assessment at advanced levels, but it should not replace the testing of facts.
Explanation, in other words, is the roof of learning, but facts remain its foundation.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that educators should assess explanation instead of factual knowledge.
Facts protect safety in high-stakes fields and allow fairer grading, while explanation earns a larger role only once that foundation is secure.
Educators should therefore assess both, moving from a [[rudimentary|rudimentary]] command of facts toward explanation only as students' knowledge grows.

essays.title: Image too often outweighs reality today

paragraphs.text: Polished images are now [[ubiquitous|ubiquitous]], and a single photograph can reach millions of people within minutes.
This power has led many observers to worry that, in contemporary society, creating an appealing image has become more important than the reality behind it.
I largely agree with this statement, particularly in online life, business and politics, although reality still tends to reassert itself where the consequences are serious.

Social media rewards appearance over substance, many institutions invest more in their image than in their quality, and, admittedly, in high-stakes fields such as medicine, reality eventually prevails.
First, the statement holds true on social media, where an attractive post spreads faster than an accurate one.
Smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011, but the same tools also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
Fact-checkers rarely catch up, because a correction is less exciting to share than the original claim.
In my own field, I have seen dramatic but false claims about miracle cures for dengue shared widely, while careful clarifications from doctors received little attention.
Similarly, many influencers present [[idyllic|idyllic]] lives that bear little relation to their daily reality.
These examples show that online, the appeal of an image often matters more than its truth, just as the statement claims.
In this setting, truth is often [[eclipsed|eclipse]] by whatever is most eye-catching.
Second, in business and politics, an appealing image is frequently treated as more valuable than the product or policy itself.
Consider a private clinic that spends heavily on a modern website, celebrity endorsements and a [[palatial|palatial]] lobby while hiring too few qualified nurses.
Patients may choose it over a plainer public hospital with better outcomes simply because it looks more trustworthy.
Likewise, politicians often hire advisers to craft slogans and photo opportunities, sometimes investing more effort in appearance than in policy.
During election campaigns, a well-produced video can attract far more attention than a detailed policy proposal.
Such cases suggest that many institutions have learned that image wins customers and votes, which explains why the statement rings true to so many people.
When rewards follow appearance, people naturally invest in appearance first.
Admittedly, the statement does not hold everywhere, because in fields where results can be measured, reality tends to win in the end.

Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, was presented as safe, but the severe birth defects it caused in thousands of babies in Europe could not be hidden, and the US passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
Nevertheless, such corrections often arrive only after serious harm has been done, which suggests that image now leads and reality follows.
Similarly, a supplement advertised online as a miracle cure can sell well for years before careful studies show that it does not work.

This consideration shapes my position: reality still matters, but the growing gap between how quickly images spread and how slowly truth is established is exactly what makes the statement largely accurate.
Reality wins eventually, but often too late for the people harmed by the image.
In conclusion, I largely agree that contemporary society often values an appealing image more than the reality behind it.
Social media spreads attractive falsehoods, institutions invest heavily in appearance, and only in measurable, high-stakes fields does reality reliably catch up.
The task for citizens, then, is to act as [[skeptics|skeptic]] who ask what lies behind every polished image before they trust it.

essays.title: Reality still outlasts the appealing image

paragraphs.text: Every generation seems to believe that appearances matter more in its own time than ever before.
The statement that creating an appealing image has become more important than the reality behind it reflects this familiar complaint.
Although image is undeniably powerful today, I mostly disagree with the statement, because in the long run, reality continues to determine success, reputation and public trust.
Organizations that lack substance eventually fail, modern tools make it easier than ever to expose false images, and, admittedly, image can win in the short term.
First, the statement does not hold for organizations, because an appealing image cannot save one whose reality has fallen behind.

Kodak, for example, was a famous brand, yet when its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, the company, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography.
No amount of brand loyalty could [[offset|offset]] that reality, and Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Similarly, a restaurant with stylish photos online but poor food may attract first-time customers, but it rarely keeps them.
In the same way, patients return to the clinic that cured them, not to the one with the most attractive advertisements.
These cases show that image may open the door, but reality decides whether anyone stays.
An appealing image, in other words, can attract attention, but only substance can sustain it.
Second, contemporary society has more tools than ever to test images against reality, which limits how far appearance alone can go.
In 2015, a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them.
Findings that had looked impressive were exposed by careful checking, and the field responded by demanding more rigorous methods.
Science, a field that might seem vulnerable to impressive headlines, thus corrected itself through patient testing.
In my own field, journals now often ask researchers to share their data so that others can check whether the results hold.
Likewise, online reviews and fact-checking websites now allow ordinary people to [[debunk|debunk]] misleading advertisements within days.
This suggests that modern society, far from abandoning truth, has developed powerful ways to [[unearth|unearth]] it.
The more easily images can be checked, the less power they have to replace the truth.
Admittedly, the strongest case for the statement is that image often wins in the short term, especially online.
Smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly during the Arab Spring of 2011, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
A false rumor about a vaccine, for example, can spread across a country in a single day.
Nevertheless, a short-term advantage is not the same as greater importance, since false images tend to collapse once their consequences become visible.
In my work in public health, for instance, rumors about dengue cures spread quickly, but they faded once patients saw that the remedies did not work.
This consideration qualifies my view: image now matters more quickly than it once did, but reality still matters more in the end.
Short bursts of attention, however intense, rarely decide the long-term fate of a product, a person or an idea.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that image has become more important than the reality behind it in contemporary society.
Organizations without substance still fail, modern tools expose false images, and image wins only in the short run.
For individuals and institutions alike, the [[prudent|prudent]] strategy remains to build something real first and to polish its image second.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1 and 2 show where the statement does not hold (failing organizations, modern fact-checking); Body 3 grants where it does hold (short-term online spread) and explains how that qualifies the position.

essays.title: Citizens' well-being is the truest test

paragraphs.text: Leaders often ask to be judged by their speeches, their monuments or the size of their armies.
A better test, according to the claim, is how well the country's citizens actually live.

I largely agree that the effectiveness of a country's leaders is best measured by the well-being of its citizens, provided that well-being is judged over a reasonable period and with attention to circumstances beyond a leader's control.

Well-being reflects the true purpose of government, it is harder to manipulate than other measures, and, although critics rightly note that leaders cannot control everything, this objection can be answered.
First, citizens' well-being is the right measure because improving people's lives is the basic purpose of leadership.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986, for instance, replaced central planning with market incentives.
A country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Those leaders are rightly judged effective because ordinary families ate better and earned more, whatever one thinks of particular policies.
Similarly, Singapore's leaders are often praised because their housing program now houses about 80% of residents, most of whom own their flats.
These cases show that when we call leaders effective, we usually mean that they [[ameliorate|ameliorate]] the lives of the people they govern, which supports the claim.
A government that builds a strong army while its people go hungry has failed at its central task.
Second, well-being is a more reliable measure than the alternatives that leaders often prefer.
Economic growth, military strength or grand buildings can rise while ordinary people suffer, as when a government builds a [[palatial|palatial]] capital while rural clinics lack basic medicines.
Measures of well-being, such as life expectancy, child mortality and access to clean water, are harder to [[embellish|embellish]] because they reflect daily life directly.
As an epidemiologist, I have often seen mortality data reveal problems that official speeches ignored.
Consider a district where rising child deaths from dengue expose weak local clinics long before officials admit any problem.
This shows that well-being provides the most honest scorecard of leadership, precisely because it focuses on outcomes rather than appearances.
Leaders who know they will be judged this way have a strong reason to invest in clinics, schools and clean water.
The most compelling challenge to this position is that citizens' well-being depends on many factors beyond leaders' control, such as natural disasters, global recessions or pandemics.
A competent government may face a sudden epidemic and see deaths rise despite wise decisions, while a careless one may simply enjoy good fortune.
Nevertheless, this objection argues for measuring well-being carefully, not for abandoning it.
Fair observers can compare a country with similar neighbors facing the same shock, or examine trends over a full term rather than a single bad year.
Thus the challenge refines my position: well-being remains the best measure as long as it is [[contextualized|contextualize]] rather than read as a simple snapshot.
Context explains a bad year; it does not excuse a decade of decline.
In conclusion, I largely agree that leaders' effectiveness is best judged by the well-being of their citizens.
This measure reflects the purpose of government and is harder to manipulate than growth figures or monuments, although it must account for forces that no leader controls.
Citizens who judge their leaders this way will reward those who improve daily life rather than those who merely promise to.

essays.title: Well-being alone misjudges a leader

paragraphs.text: A ship's captain who steers through a storm may arrive late, yet still deserve credit for saving everyone on board.
The claim that leaders' effectiveness is best measured by the well-being of citizens overlooks this kind of distinction.

Although citizens' well-being matters greatly, I mostly disagree that it is the best measure of a leader's effectiveness, because it reflects many forces beyond a leader's control and often reveals the effects of decisions only years later.
Well-being is shaped by luck and inheritance, good decisions often pay off long after a leader leaves office, and, admittedly, well-being remains the ultimate goal of good government.
First, citizens' well-being is a poor measure of a leader's effectiveness because it depends heavily on factors no leader controls.
Consider two health ministers during a pandemic.

One governs a wealthy country with many hospitals, while the other inherits [[rudimentary|rudimentary]] clinics and few doctors; even if the second minister acts more wisely, her citizens may still suffer more.
Similarly, a leader whose country is struck by a drought or a global recession may see incomes fall despite [[judicious|judicious]] policies.
These cases show that well-being often measures circumstances and economic [[vicissitudes|vicissitude]] as much as leadership, so using it alone would reward luck and punish misfortune.
Judging leaders this way would be like blaming a doctor for a disease that was already advanced when the patient arrived.
Second, effective decisions often improve well-being only long after the leader who made them has left office.
Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms of 1986 replaced central planning with market incentives, but poverty fell dramatically over the following decades rather than within a single term.
Judged by citizens' well-being in the first few years, the leaders who began these reforms might have looked far less effective than they were.

Likewise, funding for basic science may seem wasteful for years, as the little-noticed mRNA research of Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman once did, before it produces benefits such as the COVID-19 vaccines.
This shows that a snapshot of well-being can [[belie|belie]] a leader's real contribution, which is why I reject the claim that it is the best measure.
Voters who judge only by present conditions may therefore punish the reformers whose work later helps them most.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that well-being is, after all, the purpose of government, so any other measure risks rewarding leaders for things that do not matter.
Singapore's housing program, which now houses about 80% of residents, most of whom own their flats, is praised precisely because it improved people's lives.
Nevertheless, agreeing that well-being is the goal does not mean that current well-being is the best measure of a particular leader's effectiveness.
A minister who builds strong public health institutions during a crisis, for example, may preside over many deaths while still saving more lives than any alternative would have.
A fairer judgment examines the quality of decisions given the circumstances, along with long-term trends, so that well-being serves as evidence rather than as the final verdict.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that citizens' well-being is the best measure of leadership, although it remains the goal that leadership should serve.
Well-being is shaped by luck and inheritance, and good decisions often bear fruit only after a leader departs.
Citizens should therefore judge leaders by the wisdom of their choices in context, not merely by the conditions over which they happen to preside.

essays.title: Require parent volunteering, flexibly

paragraphs.text: A school can hire teachers and buy books, but it cannot buy the involvement of families.
For this reason, some argue that all parents should be required to volunteer time to their children's schools.
I agree with this claim, as long as the requirement is modest and flexible enough for parents with demanding jobs to meet it in different ways.

Parental volunteering improves children's learning, it builds a school community that benefits everyone, and, although critics rightly worry about burdening poorer families, a flexible requirement can address that concern.
First, requiring parents to volunteer is justified because their involvement directly improves children's learning and behavior.
Consider a primary school in Hanoi where every parent must give a few hours each term, whether by reading with students, helping in the library or organizing a science fair.
Children see that their parents value school, teachers gain extra help, and parents learn what their children are studying, so they can support homework more effectively.
Similarly, a parent who has spent a morning in a crowded classroom is far less likely to dismiss a teacher's concerns about a child's behavior.

These benefits explain why a requirement, rather than a polite invitation, is warranted: the parents who [[abstain|abstain]] when volunteering is optional are often those whose children would gain the most.
Volunteering, in this sense, is less a favor to the school than an investment in one's own child.
Second, mandatory volunteering builds a school community in which responsibility is shared rather than left to a few.
In many schools, a small [[coterie|coterie]] of enthusiastic parents does nearly all the work, while most families remain distant.
A requirement spreads the burden, brings in parents with varied skills, and reduces the resentment that builds when the same few people always volunteer.
As a physician, for example, I could give a short talk on handwashing or dengue prevention, a contribution that costs me little but teaches children something useful.
Similarly, an engineer could help with a science project, and a farmer could show students how rice is grown.
This shows that requiring every family to contribute turns a school from a service that parents consume into a community that they help build.
Shared work also builds trust between teachers and families, which makes later problems easier to solve.
The most compelling challenge to this position is that a requirement would burden low-income parents, such as factory workers or farmers who cannot leave their jobs without losing wages.
A single mother working two shifts may simply be unable to visit the school during the day.
If the rule demanded weekday visits only, it would punish her for her poverty rather than help her child.
Nevertheless, this concern argues for a flexible requirement, not for abolishing it.
Schools can let parents contribute on weekends, from home or by sharing a skill, and they can excuse families facing genuine hardship.
With such options, the requirement becomes [[equitable|equitable]] rather than [[onerous|onerous]], and its benefits for children remain intact.
The challenge, then, improves the policy rather than defeating it.
In conclusion, I agree that all parents should be required to volunteer time to their children's schools, provided the requirement is modest and flexible.
Such volunteering improves children's learning and builds a shared school community, and flexible options can protect families with limited time.
A well-designed requirement asks every parent for something, but it never asks any parent for the impossible.

essays.task_note: Body 3 states the strongest challenge (the burden on low-income parents), concedes it, and answers it with a flexible requirement and hardship exemptions.

essays.title: Encourage parent volunteering, never require it

paragraphs.text: Good intentions can turn into unfair rules when they ignore people's real lives.
The claim that all parents should be required to volunteer time to their children's schools is a clear example.

Although parental involvement benefits children, I mostly disagree with this claim, because a universal requirement would burden the families least able to comply and would produce reluctant rather than meaningful help.
A mandate would fall hardest on poor and overworked parents, forced volunteering tends to be shallow, and, admittedly, schools do lose out when parents stay away.
First, a requirement would be unfair because parents differ greatly in the time and resources they have.
Consider a factory worker in an industrial zone near Ho Chi Minh City who works long shifts six days a week and lives far from her child's school.
Requiring her to volunteer would force her either to lose wages or to break the rule, while a wealthy parent with flexible hours would comply easily.
Even a few hours each term could mean a lost day's pay that her family cannot afford.
Similarly, parents who are ill, care for elderly relatives or raise children alone would face a burden that the rule's authors may never have imagined.
These cases show that a universal requirement would [[exacerbate|exacerbate]] existing inequalities and might even [[stigmatize|stigmatize]] children whose parents cannot take part.
A rule meant to help children would end up penalizing those who already have the least.
Second, compulsory volunteering would likely produce shallow participation rather than the engaged support that actually helps children.
Anyone who has supervised mandatory training knows that people forced to attend often do the minimum, watching the clock instead of contributing.
In my experience running training sessions for health workers, those who came only because attendance was compulsory asked the fewest questions.
Parents required to spend a few hours at school might likewise offer [[perfunctory|perfunctory]] help that adds little to children's learning.
By contrast, Wikipedia, written by unpaid volunteers who chose to contribute, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
Its success came from people who wanted to share what they knew, not from people ordered to write.
This suggests that much of the value of volunteering comes from its voluntary nature, which a requirement would destroy.
Help that is demanded tends to be minimal, while help that is invited is often generous.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that, without a requirement, many parents who could help simply do not.
In many schools, a small group of parents organizes every event while others remain distant, and children of uninvolved parents may miss out.
Nevertheless, the better response is to make participation easier and more attractive, not to make it compulsory.
Schools can offer evening events, short tasks that can be done from home, or invitations to share professional skills, which draw in many parents without punishing those who cannot come.
This challenge therefore shapes my view: parental involvement is worth pursuing actively, but through [[incentives|incentive]] and invitation rather than obligation.
Such an approach keeps the benefits of involvement without its unfairness.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that all parents should be required to volunteer at their children's schools.
A mandate would burden the families with the least time, and forced help tends to be shallow, even though parental involvement is valuable.
Schools will gain more by welcoming parents in flexible ways than by turning goodwill into a duty.

essays.title: A shared national core serves every student

paragraphs.text: Where a child is born should not decide what that child has the chance to learn.
This principle supports the claim that a nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.
I largely agree with this claim, provided that the common curriculum sets a shared core of knowledge while leaving teachers room to adapt how it is taught.

A national curriculum promotes equal opportunity, it creates a shared foundation for citizens, and, although critics argue that it ignores local needs and stifles creativity, this risk can be managed.
First, a common curriculum promotes fairness because it guarantees that rural and poor students are taught the same essential content as wealthy urban students.
In Vietnam, a student in a mountain district and a student in central Hanoi follow the same national program, so both are prepared for the same university entrance examinations.
Without that shared standard, schools in poorer areas might quietly lower their expectations, leaving their students with a disadvantage they could never [[surmount|surmount]].
Similarly, a child whose family moves from one province to another can continue learning without gaps or repetition.
This continuity matters in a country where many families move to cities in search of work.
These cases show that a national curriculum makes education more [[equitable|equitable]], which is the strongest reason to require it for all students.
Equal content does not guarantee equal results, but it removes one important source of inequality.
Second, a shared curriculum gives citizens a common foundation of knowledge, which a nation needs in order to function as a community.
When every student learns the same basic biology, for instance, public health campaigns about vaccination or dengue prevention can build on knowledge that the whole population shares.
In my work on disease control, explaining risk is far easier when people already understand how infections spread.
Likewise, a common history course gives young people from different regions a shared story and a common vocabulary for discussing their country's future.
This shows that a national curriculum does more than transmit facts; it helps citizens from different backgrounds [[coalesce|coalesce]] into a society that can understand one another.
Such shared understanding is difficult to build if every school teaches entirely different content.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that a single curriculum may ignore local needs and limit creativity.
Finland, often admired for its schools, gives its highly trained teachers considerable freedom and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Nevertheless, this example shows the value of flexible teaching methods, not the danger of shared content, since Finland still sets national goals for what students should learn.
A national curriculum can likewise define core subjects while allowing schools to add local languages, crafts or electives.
This challenge therefore refines my position: the content of the core should be national, but the methods and the extras should remain local.
Shared goals and local freedom, in other words, are not opposites but partners.
In conclusion, I largely agree that all students should study the same national curriculum before college, as long as it defines a core rather than [[circumscribing|circumscribe]] every lesson.
A common curriculum promotes equal opportunity and a shared civic foundation, and flexibility in teaching can answer the concern about local needs.
Such a balance gives every child the same starting line without forcing every classroom into the same mold.

essays.title: One curriculum cannot fit every student

paragraphs.text: Students form a [[heterogeneous|heterogeneous]] group, differing in talents, interests and goals as much as in height.
Yet the claim holds that a nation should require all of its students to study the same national curriculum until they enter college.

Although some shared standards are useful, I mostly disagree with this claim, because a single required curriculum ignores students' different needs and discourages the variety that drives better teaching.
A uniform curriculum fails students with different abilities and goals, it limits teachers' freedom to innovate, and, admittedly, common standards do help ensure fairness.
First, a single curriculum fails many students because it assumes that all of them need the same knowledge at the same pace.
Consider a sixteen-year-old in rural Vietnam who wants to become a mechanic or a farmer using modern techniques.
Requiring him to follow exactly the same academic program as a student preparing for medical school may leave him bored, unprepared for his chosen work and more likely to drop out.
Vocational programs in many countries keep such students engaged by linking lessons to real jobs.
Similarly, a student gifted in mathematics may lose interest when forced to [[dawdle|dawdle]] at the pace set for everyone else.
These cases show that uniformity, however well meant, can [[impede|impede]] the very students it claims to serve.
A curriculum that serves the average student well may serve the individual student poorly.
Second, a required national curriculum limits innovation by preventing schools and teachers from trying new approaches.
Finland, often admired for its schools, requires teachers to hold a master's degree and then trusts them with considerable freedom, relying far less on standardized testing than many countries.
This trust allows teachers to adjust lessons to the students in front of them rather than follow a script set by distant officials.

Likewise, the Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, learned through their own experiments with gliders and a homemade wind tunnel, a reminder that valuable learning often happens outside a fixed program.
This suggests that a nation benefits more from many experiments in teaching than from a single, [[ossified|ossify]] curriculum.
If one method fails, a nation with many methods can learn from the others; a nation with one method cannot.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that, without a common curriculum, schools in poor areas may offer weaker education, widening inequality.
In many countries, wealthy districts can afford richer programs, while poorer schools struggle to teach even basic subjects.
Wealthier families can also pay for private tutoring, which widens the gap further.
Nevertheless, this problem can be solved with national minimum standards in core subjects such as reading, mathematics and science, rather than with one curriculum for every subject and every year.
Vietnam, for example, could keep a national standard in core subjects while letting schools design vocational and advanced courses for different students.
This challenge therefore shapes my position: the state should guarantee a floor of essential knowledge, but above that floor, students and schools should be free to choose their own paths.
Fairness requires a common minimum, not a common maximum.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that every student should follow the same national curriculum until college.
Such uniformity fails students with different goals and limits innovation, while the legitimate concern for fairness can be met by minimum standards.
A nation serves its young people best by setting a common foundation and then allowing many different paths to be built on it.

essays.title: Require a semester abroad, and fund it

paragraphs.text: Some lessons cannot be learned from a textbook, only from living among people who see the world differently.
This is the main argument for the claim that colleges and universities should require their students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.
I largely agree with this claim, as long as universities provide financial support so that the requirement does not exclude poorer students.
Studying abroad builds the international outlook that modern problems demand, it develops independence and adaptability, and, although cost is a serious objection, it can be addressed.
First, a semester abroad is valuable because many of today's most important problems cross national borders.
The eradication of smallpox, declared in 1980, depended on a coordinated WHO campaign in which countries shared data and vaccine.
The people who led such efforts needed to understand other countries' health systems, languages and customs.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, also showed how much researchers from different countries can achieve together.

Similarly, antibiotic resistance spreads today partly through the overuse and over-the-counter sale of antibiotics in many countries, including Vietnam, so tackling it requires professionals who can work across borders.
These cases show that global problems demand an international outlook, and a required semester abroad is one reliable way to [[engender|engender]] it.
Graduates who have lived abroad are better prepared to join such cooperation.
Second, living in a foreign country develops independence and adaptability that classroom learning rarely provides.
Consider a Vietnamese medical student who spends a semester at a hospital in another country.
She must work in an unfamiliar language, adapt to different routines and ask for help, and she returns with greater confidence and a broader view of how health care can be organized.
Likewise, a business student who spends a semester abroad learns firsthand that markets and customers differ, a lesson that no case study conveys as vividly.
In my experience, colleagues who trained abroad adapt quickly to new teams and unfamiliar problems.
Such experiences make students less [[insular|insular]] and more [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]], qualities that employers and societies increasingly need.
These are skills that matter in every career, not only in international ones.
The most compelling challenge to this position is cost: travel, housing and tuition abroad can be [[prohibitive|prohibitive]] for students from poor families.
A student from a farming family in the Mekong Delta might be unable to pay for a semester in Europe, and a strict requirement could even prevent her from graduating.
Even with a partial scholarship, airfare and rent in a foreign city could exceed what her family can manage.
Nevertheless, this problem argues for funding the requirement, not for abandoning it.
Universities can offer scholarships, sign exchange agreements that keep tuition at home rates, and partner with nearby countries where living costs are lower.
This challenge therefore shapes my position: the requirement is justified only when universities make it affordable for every student.
A requirement without funding would be unjust, but a funded requirement would open doors that many students could never open alone.
In conclusion, I largely agree that universities should require students to study abroad for at least one semester, provided they make it financially possible for all.
Such a semester prepares graduates for global problems and builds independence, while scholarships and exchanges can answer the concern about cost.
A requirement backed by real support would turn a privilege of the few into an opportunity for everyone.
