essays.title: Encourage study abroad, but do not require it

paragraphs.text: An experience that transforms one student may be a heavy burden for another.
This is the main problem with the claim that colleges and universities should require all students to spend at least one semester studying in a foreign country.

Although studying abroad can be valuable, I mostly disagree that it should be required, because a universal mandate would be unfair to many students and is unnecessary for gaining international understanding.
The requirement would exclude students with limited money or heavy responsibilities, its benefits can be achieved in other ways, and, admittedly, time abroad does offer real advantages.
First, a required semester abroad would be unfair because many students cannot afford it or cannot leave home.
Consider a student in Vietnam whose parents are farmers and who works part-time to pay her tuition; a semester in another country could cost more than her family earns in a year.
Other students care for sick relatives, have children of their own, or have disabilities that make travel difficult.
Similarly, students in demanding programs such as medicine may find that a semester abroad delays their clinical training and graduation.
A requirement that ignores these situations would force some students to choose between their families and their degrees.
For such students, the requirement would be not an opportunity but an [[onerous|onerous]] barrier, which [[undermines|undermine]] the claim that it should apply to everyone.
A rule that only some students can meet is not a fair graduation requirement.
Second, the benefits of studying abroad can often be achieved without leaving one's own country.
International collaboration increasingly happens online and in mixed teams at home.
Many of my own international collaborations in epidemiology, for instance, began with online meetings rather than travel.

The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers, so a student almost anywhere can now take part in global science.
Likewise, universities can invite visiting professors, enroll international students and offer joint online courses, bringing foreign perspectives to students who stay home.
This suggests that a mandate is unnecessary, since the goal of a [[cosmopolitan|cosmopolitan]] education can be reached by many [[feasible|feasible]] paths.
Universities can therefore pursue international understanding without making travel compulsory.
The most compelling challenge to my position is that living abroad teaches lessons that no online course can, such as independence and the ability to adapt to an unfamiliar culture.
A medical student who spends a semester in a foreign hospital, for instance, must solve daily problems in another language and returns with a confidence that is hard to gain at home.
Nevertheless, recognizing these benefits supports encouraging and funding study abroad, not forcing it on every student.
Scholarships, exchange agreements and short summer programs can bring these experiences within reach of students who want them.

This challenge therefore shapes my position: universities should make study abroad widely available through scholarships and exchanges, while allowing students to choose it when it fits their circumstances.
Choice, not compulsion, is what makes such experiences meaningful.
In conclusion, I mostly disagree that universities should require every student to study abroad.
Such a requirement would burden students with limited resources, and international understanding can also be gained at home, even though time abroad has real value.
Universities should therefore open the door to study abroad as widely as possible, without pushing every student through it.

essays.title: Guiding students toward jobs helps everyone

paragraphs.text: Graduating with a degree but no job is one of the most discouraging experiences a young person can face.
To prevent it, some propose that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.
I support this policy, as long as encouragement means giving students clear information and incentives rather than forbidding them to follow other interests.

The policy would reduce graduate unemployment, it would help societies meet urgent needs, and, although it might discourage some talented students from less practical fields, that consequence can be limited.
First, implementing the policy would likely reduce unemployment and wasted investment among graduates.
In Vietnam, many families make great sacrifices to send their children to university, yet some graduates in crowded fields struggle for years to find work related to their degree.
If schools showed students data on job prospects before they chose a major, more of them could enter fields where their effort would be rewarded.
Graduates with stable jobs can also repay their families' sacrifices, a responsibility many young Vietnamese take seriously.
Similarly, a student who learns early that demand for nurses or data analysts is high may choose a path that leads to stable employment and independence.
This consequence strongly shapes my support, because a policy that spares young people [[futile|futile]] years of searching for work is a [[pragmatic|pragmatic]] form of care.
Students remain free to choose, but they choose with better knowledge.
Second, the policy would help societies meet their most [[pressing|pressing]] needs.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, countries with too few nurses, laboratory technicians and epidemiologists struggled to test and treat patients.
In my own work in public health, I have seen a shortage of trained staff delay a dengue response even when money and equipment were available.
When jobs go unfilled in such fields, patients wait longer and outbreaks spread further.
Likewise, as smartphones and digital services spread, societies need far more engineers and programmers than they once did.
This shows that guiding students toward fields with plentiful jobs serves not only individuals but also the public, since those jobs are plentiful precisely because the work is needed.
Encouraging students to fill such gaps is therefore a public good as well as a private benefit.

Admittedly, the policy could have a negative consequence: talented students might be discouraged from fields such as art, history or basic science, where jobs are scarce but contributions can be [[profound|profound]].
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.
A policy that steered every young artist toward accounting might have cost the world such work.
Nevertheless, this risk arises only if encouragement becomes pressure, and a well-designed policy can avoid that.
Schools can provide job information and scholarships for high-demand fields while still supporting students who, fully informed, choose a different path.
This consequence therefore qualifies my support: the policy is beneficial as long as it informs students' choices rather than dictating them.
Information widens choices; only coercion would narrow them.
In conclusion, I support encouraging students to choose fields with plentiful jobs, provided the encouragement respects their freedom.
Such a policy would reduce graduate unemployment and help meet urgent social needs, and its risks to less practical fields can be limited.
Clear information, offered early, allows students to follow their interests with open eyes rather than discover the job market too late.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1 and 2 trace positive consequences of implementing the policy; Body 3 weighs a negative consequence (lost talent in arts and basic science) and explains how it limits the support.

essays.title: Steering students toward jobs can backfire

paragraphs.text: The job market of today is rarely the job market of tomorrow.
This uncertainty raises doubts about the policy that educational institutions should actively encourage students to choose fields of study in which jobs are plentiful.

Although students deserve accurate information about careers, I oppose this policy, because steering them toward currently popular fields would likely create future surpluses, waste individual talent and neglect work whose value appears only later.
Job markets change faster than degrees can be completed, students do their best work in fields that suit them, and, admittedly, the policy could reduce short-term unemployment.
First, implementing the policy could backfire because today's plentiful jobs may become tomorrow's crowded fields.

If every school pushed students toward a profession that is in demand today, large numbers of graduates might enter the market at the same time several years later, when demand may already have fallen.
Students who chose a field for its job prospects alone would then face the very unemployment that the policy was meant to prevent.
In my own field, for instance, the demand for epidemiologists rose sharply during the COVID-19 pandemic and then eased once the emergency passed.
Kodak's story shows how quickly an industry can change: its engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, yet the company clung to film and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
These consequences suggest that the policy rests on a [[myopic|myopic]] view of the job market, which is one reason I oppose it.
Guidance based on today's vacancies may simply move unemployment a few years into the future.
Second, the policy would likely waste talent, because students perform best in fields that match their abilities and interests.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics and chemistry despite the barriers women faced in science at the time, a career few advisers would have called a safe choice.
Her achievements came from [[ardent|ardent]] commitment to her subject, not from a calculation about available jobs.
Likewise, Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman spent decades on little-noticed mRNA research, work that later made rapid COVID-19 vaccines possible and won the 2023 Nobel Prize.
This consequence shapes my opposition: a policy that pushes students away from their interests would [[sap|sap]] the motivation that produces excellence.
Societies need such people, and they rarely appear on lists of plentiful jobs.
Admittedly, the policy could reduce short-term unemployment and help students avoid degrees that lead nowhere.
In Vietnam, some families invest heavily in degrees that leave graduates searching for work for years, and clearer guidance might prevent such losses.
Nevertheless, this benefit can be achieved by giving students honest information about job prospects rather than actively steering them.
A university that publishes employment rates for each program and offers career counseling respects students' choices while still protecting them from uninformed decisions.
This consequence therefore refines my position: institutions should inform students, but they should not encourage them to [[abdicate|abdicate]] their own judgment in favor of the latest job report.
Honest information protects students; active steering replaces their judgment with someone else's.
In conclusion, I oppose the policy of actively encouraging students to choose fields in which jobs are plentiful.
It could create future surpluses, waste talent and neglect fields whose value emerges slowly, while its benefits can be gained through honest career information.
Schools serve students best by informing their choices, not by making those choices for them.

essays.task_note: Bodies 1 and 2 trace harmful consequences of implementing the policy (future gluts, lost talent); Body 3 weighs a benefit (less short-term unemployment) and explains how it shapes the position toward information rather than steering.

bank: Ignaz Semmelweis (Vienna, 1847) had doctors wash their hands in chlorinated lime; deaths from childbed fever on his ward fell sharply, yet most colleagues rejected his idea, which germ theory vindicated only years after his death.

Alexander Fleming noticed in 1928 that mold killed bacteria on a culture plate; penicillin became a usable drug only when Howard Florey and Ernst Chain's team developed it during World War II. In his 1945 Nobel lecture Fleming warned that misuse would breed resistant bacteria.

Antibiotic resistance today: overuse and over-the-counter sales of antibiotics, common in many countries including Vietnam, help resistant bacteria spread, so drugs that once cured infections now often fail.
Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 after a coordinated global WHO vaccination campaign that relied on countries sharing data and vaccine.

The COVID-19 mRNA vaccines were developed in under a year because of decades of earlier, little-noticed basic research on mRNA by Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, who won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

Thalidomide, a sedative given to pregnant women around 1960, caused severe birth defects in thousands of babies in Europe; Frances Kelsey of the US FDA refused to approve it, and the US then passed stricter drug-testing rules in 1962.
The Tuskegee syphilis study (1932-1972) withheld treatment from Black men without their informed consent; the public outrage led to US rules requiring ethics review boards for research on people.

Wolbachia mosquitoes: releasing mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia bacteria, which block dengue transmission, cut dengue cases by 77% in a randomized trial in Yogyakarta, Indonesia; the method has also been tested in Vietnam.
Vietnam's 2007 law requiring motorbike helmets raised helmet use from low levels to over 90% within months and reduced head injuries and deaths.

Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms (1986) replaced central planning with market incentives; a country that had faced food shortages became one of the world's largest rice exporters, and poverty fell dramatically over the following decades.
Galileo was forced by the Church in 1633 to recant his support for the idea that the Earth moves around the sun.
The Human Genome Project, a publicly funded international effort completed in 2003, made the human DNA sequence freely available to all researchers.
In 2015 a large collaboration tried to repeat 100 published psychology studies and reproduced the results of only about a third of them, revealing how often single findings mislead.
GPS was built by the US military; once it was opened to civilians, it became the basis of everyday navigation, ride-hailing and delivery apps.
Kodak engineer Steven Sasson invented the digital camera in 1975, but Kodak, protecting its profitable film business, was slow to embrace digital photography and filed for bankruptcy in 2012.
Wikipedia, launched in 2001 and written by unpaid volunteers, grew into the largest encyclopedia in history.
Abraham Lincoln appointed his political rivals, including William Seward, to his cabinet, choosing able critics over loyal followers.
Vincent van Gogh sold very few paintings during his lifetime and is now regarded as one of the greatest painters in history.

The Wright brothers, bicycle makers without college degrees, achieved the first powered airplane flight in 1903 after years of careful experiments with gliders and a wind tunnel they built themselves.
Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in both physics (1903) and chemistry (1911) despite the barriers women faced in science at the time.
The Montgomery bus boycott (1955-1956), in which Black residents refused for over a year to ride segregated buses, helped end bus segregation in that city.
Finland requires schoolteachers to hold a master's degree, makes teaching a respected and selective profession, and relies far less on standardized testing than many countries.
Singapore's government housing program now houses about 80% of the country's residents, most of whom own their flats.
Smartphones and social media let activists organize quickly, as during the Arab Spring of 2011, but they also spread misinformation faster than corrections can follow.
